10.label: Piracy
10.nativeMeaning: GoA2 treats free seafaring, sea raiding, wealth and reverence for deep-sea creatures as a faith. Its local space can consequently be a freebooters’ hall rather than a formal clergy-led temple.
10.sourceDecision: A crew-and-prize hall with a deep-sea offering nook can spread with this maritime creed, including inland supply settlements. The religious nook is honest extrapolation from the native description, not a documented uniform pirate liturgy.

scenes.label: The Freebooters’ Prize Hall
scenes.availability: the locality follows Piracy. Public gathering hall or sheltered supply-house in a settlement following Piracy; waterfront preferable but not required. Adapt to current local seafaring connections and ordinary stored goods. No named pirate fleet, compulsory crime, bound deep-sea creature or universal binding pirate law is implied.
scenes.art: Create a swaggering freebooters’ gathering hall around a scarred crew table, route charts and a pair of prize scales. Mixed pennants, patched sailcloth and sea-chest hardware crowd the overhead beams. A half-shadowed niche bears an immense-toothed deep-sea creature carved around a ledge of coins and tiny ship tokens. Light catches brass fittings and scratched drinking cups; supply bundles and worn weapons occupy the side racks. Preserve the local culture’s ordinary construction beneath the maritime clutter. A table end and side alcove allow a visitor to bargain while others use the hall. The religious identity lies in freedom, spoils and the feared depths rather than cathedral solemnity.
contexts: Route charts cover the scarred table beside prize scales and scratched cups. Mixed pennants hang over sea chests pushed against the wall. In a dark niche, a toothy creature of the depths curls around a ledge of coins and little ship tokens. Crews use the hall to compare routes, divide returns and make agreements beyond a distant monarch’s reach. A clear table end receives visitors, while the alcove holds a quieter place for bargaining. Light glints across the offering coins beneath the carved teeth, beside a chart marked with routes into the open sea.
scenes.adaptation: Local craft supplies the hall and ships shown in its maps. Landlocked faithful use the space for crews, routes and supplies; the sea-creature niche recalls a faith carried inland.
scenes.purpose: Crew recruitment, bargaining, division of returns, route planning and maritime offerings.
scenes.lore: Native Piracy establishes freedom, raiding, wealth and deep-sea veneration. Warcraft’s pirate havens, notably Freehold, provide the communal hall and loose-authority setting.
scenes.extrapolation: A recurring prize hall and deep-sea offering niche are authored. A single standardized pirate religion, mandatory tithe or supernatural sea pact is not claimed.

10.label: Shen'dralar
10.nativeMeaning: Shen’dralar in GoA2 seek divinity through arcane study and understanding the Titans’ material Order. Scholarship is the devotional work; a portable scene should express rigorous arcane inquiry and ordered knowledge. Native aniconism supports diagrams and instruments rather than humanoid divine statuary.
10.sourceDecision: An arcane study hall is well grounded. Portable venues need ordinary books, diagrams and instruments rather than a duplicate Athenaeum, demon prison or immortality source.

scenes.label: The Hall of Ordered Arcane Study
scenes.availability: the locality follows Shen'dralar. Local study room, archive alcove or scholarly courtyard serving a Shen’dralar locality. Scale the library to the locality. Apparatus can be physical models and reference instruments; a functioning power font, bound demon or magical experiment requires actual current context.
scenes.art: Build a scholarly devotional room around orderly libram shelves and a central table of nested geometric rings. Blue-violet diagrams map correspondences between material substance and arcane law; small reference crystals and carefully labeled specimens stand beside writing tools. Repeated rectilinear framing and circular measuring forms evoke the Titans’ Order without reproducing a Titan machine. Leave a marked demonstration patch and a visitor’s writing place outside the main experiment area. Local architecture supports this intellectual sanctuary, from carved dwarven stone to timber rafters or elegant elven arches. Warm reading lamps should reveal meticulous notes and worn bindings, making the pursuit of divinity feel like sustained work.
contexts: Librams fill ranked shelves above labeled specimens and reference crystals. Nested rings occupy the central table beside diagrams of arcane relationships. A measured floor patch gives a scholar room to demonstrate a principle, while the visitor’s writing place remains clear of the instruments. Here the Shen’dralar pursuit of divinity passes through study: understanding the Order built into the material world. Lamplight picks out revisions in the notes and wear along the bindings. Questions, disputed interpretations and borrowed knowledge all have a place at the smaller desk.
scenes.adaptation: Architecture remains local. Preserve ranked shelving, measured geometry and blue-violet arcane notation; a rural school can carry the same creed with a shelf, model and chalked floor.
scenes.purpose: Scholarly reception, arcane instruction, intellectual disputes and knowledge exchange.
scenes.lore: Native theology joins arcane inquiry to Titan Order and divinity. The canonical Shen’dralar are arcanists with a major library and lorekeepers. The faith-level tenets include aniconism and astrology; abstract geometry and celestial study are appropriate.
scenes.extrapolation: Widespread small study halls, Titan-order diagram programs and modest physical models are an extrapolation from the mod’s doctrine. Immol’thar imprisonment belongs to Eldre’Thalas history and is not generalized.

10.label: Belorism
10.nativeMeaning: Belorism is mostly secular arcane reverence for the Sun, with prayer emerging in dark times. Its ordinary scene should join solar symbolism to practiced arcane life without assuming a Holy Light theology or reproducing the Sunwell.
10.sourceDecision: A small sun-facing arcane court or sheltered solar study space can spread with the faith. Its images honor a source of power; they do not themselves create a new source.

scenes.label: The Sun-Facing Arcane Court
scenes.availability: the locality follows Belorism. Courtyard, roof terrace or east-facing study shelter in a Belorist settlement. Use an available sun-facing opening or symbolic sun panel indoors. The scene is valid through ordinary local faith; actual original Sunwell, later purification or rare arcane supply cannot be inferred.
scenes.art: Compose a sun-facing arcane court around a radiant sun disk, with red cloth and gold-toned fittings warming the locality’s ordinary architecture. A lens stand and a table of arcane notes occupy the brighter side; a chalked practice ring leaves open floor nearby. A small protected ledge holds tokens and occasional petitions beneath the disk. Keep the space cultivated and confident, suitable for a mostly secular magical tradition whose reverence can become prayer in adversity. Local stone, timber or tented cloth supplies the structure. An indoor version can use an eastern window and a painted disk; the sunlight remains ordinary rather than a copied Sunwell torrent.
contexts: Light reaches the lens stand beneath a radiant sun disk. Arcane notes lie on the worktable beside a clear practice ring, while red cloth warms the sheltered wall. Tokens and folded petitions occupy a small ledge below the image. Most work here concerns the Sun as a source of arcane power; in a darker hour, the same place can receive a prayer. The court offers room for instruction, comparison of techniques or a quiet appeal. The lens stand, petition ledge and practice ring share the same radiant emblem, with a clear speaking place between the worktable and the sheltered wall.
scenes.adaptation: Gold-red accents and sun geometry are portable; local building craft remains visible. Forest and cold-climate variants use a clear window or covered sun-facing opening rather than importing Eversong’s climate.
scenes.purpose: Arcane instruction, solar observation, occasional prayer and social meetings among faithful practitioners.
scenes.lore: The GoA2 description expressly makes the faith mostly secular and solar-arcane. Sunwell lore supports sun imagery and the centrality of arcane power, without establishing a standardized Belorist shrine.
scenes.extrapolation: The recurring solar court, lens station and modest petition niche are authored from the native creed. This template never copies the original Sunwell or its later holy/arcane restoration.

10.nativeMeaning: Shal’danalism preserves ancient arcane ways and reverence for the Nightwell, including real dependence and transformation among historically affected followers. Its local venue should convey preserved arcane sophistication and attention to sustenance without making every convert biologically dependent.
10.sourceDecision: A Nightwell remembrance and arcane salon is portable; a Nightwell-powered ration house is not universally portable. Real arcwine, hunger states and power distribution remain current campaign facts.

scenes.label: The Nightwell’s Arcane Salon
scenes.availability: the locality follows Shal'danalism. Local receiving salon, meeting chamber or small arcane guild room in a Shal’danalist settlement. Show a symbolic Nightwell design and ordinary ceremonial cups. Actual arcwine supply or distribution requires current local availability; this scene neither creates a Nightwell nor assigns withdrawal to an adopted faith’s participants.
scenes.art: Render a refined local arcane salon with violet cloth, silver-edged concentric rings and a relief of a rising font above a long display table. Patterned cups sit in ordered racks beside lineage records and preserved spell diagrams. A circular inlay establishes a demonstration area, while paired chairs or locally appropriate seats face the receiving table. The Nightwell is present as remembered geometry and revered source, not as an actual second well. Use the locality’s structure beneath the elegant overlay, from stout masonry to carved timber. Ordinary lamplight should catch polished cups and carefully tended fabrics, expressing a civilization’s insistence on maintaining ancient arcane forms.
contexts: Concentric silver-edged rings surround the image of a rising font above the display table. Patterned cups stand in ordered racks beside lineage records and carefully preserved spell diagrams. Violet cloth softens the receiving space around a circular floor inlay. The salon keeps the Nightwell and the old arcane ways close through formal conversation, instruction and remembered tradition. An ordinary serving tray rests beneath the cup racks, close to the receiving seats where hospitality and the arcane sustenance of earlier generations enter conversation. Visitors can examine a record or speak from the paired seats beyond the demonstration ring.
scenes.adaptation: Local culture sets shell and seating. Refined violet cloth, curved ring geometry and a restrained ancient-arcane display preserve the creed through human halls, dwarven chambers or other adopted building styles.

10.label: Al'Akirism
10.nativeMeaning: GoA2 emphasizes Al’Akir’s intelligence, subtle strategy and mastery of destructive or protective winds. His local shrine should honor the commanding sky and the interpretation of changing winds rather than simply copy a thunder god’s hall. Native declarations also include human sacrifice, warmongering and taxation of nonbelievers, giving the otherwise subtle sky creed a demanding and coercive institutional side.
10.sourceDecision: An open-sky wind court is a reasonable portable elemental shrine. Skywall’s floating palaces and djinn remain specific magical settings; ordinary ground-supported shrines convey the creed.

scenes.label: The Windlord’s Tribute Court
scenes.availability: the locality follows Al'Akirism. Roof terrace, exposed courtyard, ridge shrine or open-sided shelter in an Al’Akirist settlement. Choose a reachable open-air or ventilated venue and safe current conditions. A grounded small court is enough; no djinn, permanent cyclone, floating platform or automatic protective wind appears. The ordinary court displays sacrifice and tribute equipment between uses. Actual victims, tribute collection or sacrifice require current action; reforms removing these practices should remove their fittings.
scenes.art: Build a grounded tribute court around Al’Akir’s upward-spiraling emblem. Directional posts carry long pennants beneath a copper vane, while an exposed sacrificial stone bears iron restraint rings and a narrow draining channel. A sheltered side counter holds tribute weights, tally boards and route sketches. Pale blue, white and gold give the air lord’s cult an austere grandeur, with local architecture remaining visible beneath the overlay. Keep the stone empty and the sky natural. The layout combines changing winds with demanded submission: petitioners stand in the exposed lane, while the tribute counter and protected planning surface sit under the custodians’ shelter.
contexts: Directional pennants stream above Al’Akir’s spiraling emblem and the empty sacrificial stone. Iron rings and a draining channel interrupt the smooth pale surface. Tribute weights and tally boards occupy the sheltered counter beside route sketches. The Windlord’s cult honors cunning dominion of the skies, with sacrifice and tribute giving that dominion a mortal price. Petitioners approach through the exposed lane; a visitor can speak beside the counter while the stone remains in view. The breeze pulls at the flags above the exposed lane, carrying their snapping cloth toward the protected tribute counter.
scenes.adaptation: Wind motifs remain light and directional while supporting walls remain local. Low desert shelters, snowy roof galleries and forest-edge courts can expose ribbons and a vane without requiring tall imported spires.
scenes.purpose: Tribute negotiation, religious petition, strategic counsel and preparation for a specifically current sacrifice.

scenes.extrapolation: The local tribute court, scales, empty sacrificial stone and planning counter are authored implementations of native doctrine. No sacrifice or coercive collection is forced on the current scene. Noncanonical World of Warcraft: Forever Al’Aketh material was excluded.

10.label: Anzuism
10.nativeMeaning: Anzuism honors the Raven God’s shade, twilight and solitary contemplation, while remembering his cursed flightlessness and opposition to Sethe. Its sacred space should protect shaded communion and preserve the talonpriest’s masked focus.
10.sourceDecision: A shaded raven sanctuary is strongly supported by devotional masks and outcast traditions; it travels without requiring an arakkoa population, Draenor forest or Anzu himself.

scenes.label: The Raven’s Shaded Sanctuary
scenes.availability: the locality follows Anzuism. Shaded grove shelter, roofed shrine or dim side chamber in an Anzuist locality. Keep the main devotional image and mask shelf protected from direct sun. Ordinary visitors can use the outer shade; actual divine communion or a masked talonpriest’s appearance follows present participants and rites.
scenes.art: Create a deep shaded sanctuary beneath close eaves or a dense canopy. A dark raven likeness watches over a shelf of elongated ritual masks, with feather-shaped screens dividing a common receiving edge from smaller contemplation places. Muted violet cloth, worn wood or local stone and a thin incense curl give the darkness texture. Keep direct sunlight at the threshold, where it catches the screen’s outer feathers without illuminating the central image. Make the layout intimate and secretive enough for the Raven God’s followers to commune, but accessible at ground level to adopted peoples. No god, prophetic apparition or copied Terokk relic occupies the frame.
contexts: Deep eaves and feather-carved screens surround the raven image in cool shade. Ritual masks rest along a sheltered shelf above an incense stand. The common receiving edge opens into smaller recesses where a voice can fall quieter. Anzu’s followers honor the Raven God through the shade and contemplation he favors; the masks recall a priesthood that shields its face from the sun. Visitors can wait near the threshold or speak within the outer shade, while the deeper places remain set apart for communion.
scenes.adaptation: Replace a forest canopy with awnings, deep eaves or a sheltered rock recess where necessary. Local materials carry the image; ritual shade and raven form remain recognizable across culture changes.
scenes.purpose: Quiet religious reception, solitary contemplation, confidential conversation and preparation for communion.
scenes.lore: Native Anzuism establishes twilight and shade. The in-game Talonpriest Mask archaeology description identifies masks as a focus for communion with Anzu and avoidance of sunlight.
scenes.extrapolation: The recurring sanctuary plan, screen carving and visitor threshold are authored. Masks are common devotional equipment, not the unique Mask of Terokk.

10.label: Sethekk
10.nativeMeaning: GoA2’s Sethekk venerate the dead god Sethe and interpret his curse as a share of divinity rather than a shame to cure. Their local space should make that inversion of conventional blessing vivid. Native human-sacrifice and sacred-shadow declarations support a dangerous ritual setting.
10.sourceDecision: A shrine of the honored curse with a prepared ritual circle is plausible and visually distinct. Actual Sethe blood and curse pools belong to specifically sourced material and cannot appear in every converted locality.

scenes.label: The Dead Serpent’s Honored-Curse Shrine
scenes.availability: the locality follows Sethekk. Covered ritual yard, underground room or secluded shrine chamber in a Sethekk locality. Use a symbolic dark bowl and prepared circle between rites. Actual Sethe blood, curse transmission, controlled Anzu or a risen dead god requires current evidence; symbolic reverence remains portable.
scenes.art: Arrange a dead wind-serpent relief above a low dark bowl, its once-sweeping wings carved as broken forms. Violet-black cloth descends behind the image into a floor ring of binding inscriptions. Ribbed serpent lines, tarnished bronze and worn claw-shaped rests give the space a severe arakkoa-derived ritual grammar without requiring actual arakkoa builders. Keep the bowl empty or filled with ordinary dark water and the circle inactive. An empty offering block with iron rings stands at the circle’s far side. A small outer ledge receives visitors outside the ring, leaving an unobstructed view of the honored broken wings. Use local stone, timber or clay to build a portable shrine where a feared curse is deliberately presented as divine inheritance.
contexts: The dead serpent’s wings break across the relief above a dark bowl. An empty offering block bears iron rings beyond the dark bowl. Binding marks form a ring on the floor, with violet-black cloth hanging beyond it. Here Sethe’s curse is honored as divine inheritance, and the broken wings are a sign of participation rather than disgrace. A low outer ledge offers a place to speak without crossing the ritual circle. The bowl and inscribed floor wait between rites. Their meaning gives visitors a stark setting for discussing affliction, allegiance or the difference between a gift and a wound.
scenes.adaptation: Local construction and body-appropriate entry remain visible. The faith carries serpent death imagery and reverence for broken flight, not an imported poisoned Draenor pool.
scenes.purpose: Religious discussion of curse, identity and divine inheritance; ritual preparation and reception outside a binding circle.
scenes.lore: Native Sethekk theology expressly venerates the curse. Sethe’s lore establishes curse-bearing blood and broken flight; Ritual Severance depicts Sethekk ritual circles. Native faith-level declarations include human sacrifice and sacred shadows.
scenes.extrapolation: The recurring relief, symbolic bowl and local sanctuary are authored. No contaminated blood supply, automatic ritual victim or successful binding is generalized.

Keep the bowl empty or filled with ordinary dark water and the circle inactive. An empty offering block with iron rings stands at the circle’s far side. A small outer ledge receives visitors outside the ring, leaving an unobstructed view of the honored broken wings. Use local stone, timber or clay to build a portable shrine where a feared curse is deliberately presented as divine inheritance.
Regional adaptation: Local construction and body-appropriate entry remain visible. The faith carries serpent death imagery and reverence for broken flight, not an imported poisoned Draenor pool.

Binding marks form a ring on the floor, with violet-black cloth hanging beyond it. Here Sethe’s curse is honored as divine inheritance, and the broken wings are a sign of participation rather than disgrace. 10.label: Rukhmarism
10.nativeMeaning: Rukhmarism honors a solar mother whose grace and Anzu’s cunning shaped her people; followers expect reunion with her in the skies after death. Solar thanks and an open relation to sky are portable without importing Skyreach’s entire political regime.
10.sourceDecision: A sun-dial devotional court has direct canon support. It scales easily from a village dial to a roof terrace and supplies more specific practice than a generic sun altar.

scenes.label: Rukhmar’s Court of Returning Light
scenes.availability: the locality follows Rukhmarism. Sunlit courtyard, roof terrace or bright open-sided shrine in a Rukhmarist locality. The dial uses ordinary daylight; an indoor version uses a window admitting direct sun. Nighttime leaves the same physical court available under lamps. The goddess, solar weapon and coercive Adherent government are not spawned.
scenes.art: Place a brass sundial in a court open to the sky, its marked hours surrounding a sweeping fiery-bird relief of Rukhmar. Gold-orange cloth and red feather-shaped inlays carry the palette of sunrise. Woven circular talismans hang on a sun-facing rail; ordinary lamps beneath it supply the nighttime illumination. Use natural daylight or the lamps according to the present hour. Keep the dial approachable, with a clear sitting edge for thanks, instruction or remembrance. Local craft supplies walls and paving, while the bird, measured hours and ritual exposure form the portable overlay. The rail and visitor edge remain grounded and accessible.
contexts: Hour marks circle the brass dial beneath Rukhmar’s fiery-bird image. Sunrise-colored cloth hangs above woven talismans along the sun-facing rail, with ordinary lamps mounted below. A clear sitting edge gives room for instruction, remembrance or a visitor’s question. The dial and rail remain visible from those seats, while the open central approach lets a speaker stand beneath the sweeping bird and address the gathered faithful.
scenes.adaptation: Ground access remains suitable to the adopted population. Local architecture holds the dial and bird imagery; exposed terraces can become sheltered courts or direct-sun window galleries in harsh climates.
scenes.purpose: Daily solar thanks, teaching, funerary remembrance and public devotional reception.

10.label: Daerism
10.nativeMeaning: Daerism finds a divine spark in every plant and animal without needing named Wild Gods. Human old-ways and harvest-witch lore supports local nature practice, but the creed can spread to other cultures without turning them into an Elunic order. Native ancestor-worship and sanctity-of-nature tenets also tie local living reverence to inherited household memory.
10.sourceDecision: A sheltered living shrine and an agricultural preparation shelter are distinct practical expressions. Both rely on local living things, and neither requires an old-growth forest everywhere.

scenes.label: The Living-Spark Shelter
scenes.availability: the locality follows Daerism. Garden margin, small grove, courtyard planter or sheltered patch of local life in a Daerist locality. Use real locally sustainable plants and signs of ordinary animals. A desert version can center a tended native plant; cold locales use a sheltered evergreen or indoor growing vessel. No spirit apparition or miraculous growth is implied.
scenes.art: Create a small sanctuary around a locally thriving plant, garden bed or cluster of old roots. Leaf and animal marks cover a modest stone or timber offering surface; Seed bowls, found feathers, water vessels and named household ancestor tokens sit close to the living focus. A curved low boundary protects the growth while leaving a clear place for conversation. The structure uses local materials and species, from a hardy desert shrub to a covered evergreen court or village hedge. Rich bark, soil, roots and hand-worn tools should make reverence tactile. This old-ways space honors divine sparks in ordinary life, with no towering magical tree needed to establish its sacred character.
contexts: The living growth stands inside a low curved boundary beside a surface marked with leaves and animals. Seeds, feathers and a water vessel occupy its sheltered edge beside household ancestor tokens. Daerists see a divine spark in these ordinary living things, and the little sanctuary gives that belief a place within the settlement. Visitors can sit beside the growth or bring a question about the land, its creatures or their own obligations. Soil and worked material remain close to the hands; the surrounding life supplies the shrine’s center.
scenes.adaptation: The species and structure follow locality. The faith recognizes divinity in the actual living beings present rather than planting a compulsory elven sacred tree.
scenes.purpose: Local animist observance, nature counsel, offerings and small community meetings.
scenes.lore: Native Daerism explicitly venerates divine sparks in every animal and plant. Harvest-witch lore supports surviving human nature practice rather than a necessary named-god pantheon. Native ancestor worship and sanctity of nature support remembrance beside living devotion.
scenes.extrapolation: The portable living sanctuary and offering objects are authored. No universal Daerist liturgy, actual animal familiar or wild-god appearance is claimed.

Use only where crops or other cultivated food plants are part of local life. The scene supplies ordinary crop care and devotional preparation; miraculous growth requires an actual rite or effect.
scenes.art: Set a covered work shelter beside a real cultivated plot. Seed drawers, local crop bundles, bundled roots and ceramic water bowls crowd a broad preparation table; an adjacent earth-marked offering surface gives the practical work a devotional center. Weathered wood, woven storage baskets and hand-fitted clay or stone emphasize generations of care. A low settle and clear path let a farmer bring a problem without trampling the beds. Use the actual local crop and culture’s building craft. The portable faith overlay lives in seed storage, living growth and the offering place, creating old human animism through useful everyday labor rather than grand druidic spectacle.
contexts: Seed drawers line the sheltered wall above bundles of the local crop. Roots and ceramic water bowls occupy the covered table beside an earth-marked offering surface. The growing plot begins beyond a clear footpath, with a low settle facing the work. Old-ways practice joins reverence for living things to the labor that feeds a settlement. A visitor can bring damaged leaves, discuss a failed crop or sit while supplies are sorted. The shelter smells of stored harvest and soil, and its devotional center remains within reach of ordinary working hands.
scenes.adaptation: Replace grain with the real local crop, including fruit, tubers or hardy greenhouse growth. Building materials and tools remain cultural; plants and agricultural use remain environmental.
scenes.purpose: Agricultural counsel, crop-care preparation, offerings and meetings with nature practitioners.

10.label: Staroverstvo
10.nativeMeaning: Staroverstvo is an old human nature faith with a strong bond to the Bear Gods, especially Ursoc as God of the Hunt. Local devotion should foreground that relationship rather than import a whole furbolg civilization.
10.sourceDecision: An Ursoc hunt shrine is a reasonable portable venue. The human-specific social tradition can be adopted elsewhere through the same bear focus and respectful hunting preparation.

scenes.label: Ursoc’s Hunt-and-Remembrance Lodge
scenes.availability: the locality follows Staroverstvo. Local gathering lodge, covered hunt shelter or courtyard shrine in a Starover locality. Use a bear likeness and ordinary hunt equipment appropriate to the local habitat. The scene does not produce Ursoc, his children, a living sacred bear, cursed trappers or Vordrassil’s taint.
scenes.art: Center a hunt-and-remembrance shelter on a heavy bear likeness of Ursoc, its broad paws framing an offering ledge. Spears, bows or local hunting implements rest beside a communal table; carved remembrance tokens and ordinary animal-shaped offerings occupy protected niches. Use warm timber, rough local stone or another adopted craft, keeping the bear’s mass and protective silhouette dominant. Leave enough space below the image for hunting counsel and stories of those who have gone before. Regional plants and actual local prey motifs connect the imported faith to its new land. Keep the shrine intimate and bodily rather than a huge furbolg tunnel or an embodied Wild God.
contexts: Ursoc’s broad paws frame the offering ledge above the communal table. Hunt implements rest along the near wall, with carved tokens kept in small remembrance niches. Starovers bring their bond with the Bear Gods here, honoring Ursoc’s place in the hunt and in their inherited stories. A clear table end receives travelers or those seeking counsel before setting out. Local prey marks share the carving with the great bear. The broad table keeps hunting counsel beneath the bear’s paws, while the remembrance niches gather quieter stories along the shelter’s side.
scenes.adaptation: Cold human timber lodge is a source expression, not a culture requirement. Clay, stone or cloth versions honor the same Bear God; prey species and hunting tools remain local.
scenes.purpose: Hunting counsel, devotional offerings, remembered lineage and communal stories.
scenes.lore: GoA2 explicitly establishes the human faith’s Bear God relationship and Ursoc’s hunt role. Ursoc lore provides the Wild God and physical shrine tradition in Grizzly Hills.
scenes.extrapolation: A repeatable local lodge and remembrance niches are authored. No canonical universal Starover ceremony or trophy requirement is claimed.

10.label: Mord'truar
10.nativeMeaning: Mord’truar serves the Lich King and connects death worship to mystical runes carved on armor and weapons. Its portable scene should be a severe devotional craft chamber, with necromantic allegiance visible in the handling of martial equipment. Native ritual cannibalism, sacred shadows and esotericism add a second, more bodily devotional practice beyond martial rune craft.
10.sourceDecision: A rune-carving sanctuary scales plausibly with the faith. A fully functioning death-knight runeforge is a specialized facility and is not automatically created in every converted village. A distinct prepared ritual-feast refectory accounts for the native cannibalism tenet without spawning victims, corpses or an ongoing meal.

scenes.label: The Death-Lord’s Rune-Carving Sanctuary
scenes.availability: the locality follows Mord'truar. Local shrine-workshop, crypt room or sheltered martial crafting chamber in a Mord’truari locality. Ordinary engraving station and worshipful imagery are sufficient. Working runeforge power, trapped souls, reanimation or named death knights require actual local facilities or current rites.
scenes.art: Design a severe shrine-workshop around a heavy work slab below a skull-crowned likeness of the Death-Lord. Rune templates, engraving chisels and armor rests occupy the near edge; dark weapon racks stand against bone-pale wall accents. Cold blue glass lamps illuminate the carved patterns with ordinary flame, leaving the rear devotional recess dimmer. Preserve the adopted culture’s armor and masonry while emphasizing the transformation of martial craft into service to death. A broad outer ledge lets visitors inspect a sheathed blade or discuss an inscription outside the central work position. This is a locality-scaled rune sanctuary, with no monumental runeforge or captive soul required.
contexts: Rune templates and engraving chisels line the work slab beneath the Death-Lord’s skull-crowned image. Armor rests stand beside dark weapon racks, their surfaces waiting for the mystical signs Mord’truari carve in service to the Lich King. Blue glass lamps pick out the strokes and metal edges. The outer ledge leaves space to lay down a sheathed blade or compare an inscription without occupying the work position. Copied inscriptions fill the smaller table beyond the slab, keeping the Death-Lord’s signs close to every discussion of martial service, allegiance and power.
scenes.adaptation: Local craft retains its shell and armor style. Bone-pale accents, black iron, death-lord emblem and rune-carving arrangement make allegiance legible without importing Acherus or Icecrown.
scenes.purpose: Rune explanation, weapon inspection, necromantic religious reception and discussions of service or authority.
scenes.lore: The native description explicitly establishes mystical weapon and armor runes. Death-knight runeforging provides martial rune craft; Warcraft III’s death altars supply a severe necromantic visual grammar.
scenes.extrapolation: Small rune-carving sanctuaries, lamps and local cult craft layouts are authored. They are not automatically functioning runeforges or Ebon Blade institutions.

scenes.art: Build a grim ceremonial refectory around a heavy communal slab, with bone-handled knives, empty covered platters and portion marks cut into the table’s edge. A skull-crowned Death-Lord image watches from the darker wall, framed by black cloth and narrow blue-glass lamps. Side shelves hold washed ritual vessels and records of the dead, while the entry gives visitors a place to wait before taking a seat. Keep the ordinary structure and seating local. The prepared setting acknowledges Mord’truar’s ritual consumption of flesh with concrete instruments and disciplined arrangement; it contains no current corpse, unwilling captive or compulsory feast.
contexts: Bone-handled knives lie beside empty covered platters on the communal slab. Portion marks line its edge beneath the Death-Lord’s skull-crowned image. Blue-glass lamps illuminate a shelf of washed dishes and records of the dead. Visitors can wait at the entry or speak along the table before any rite begins. The covered platters leave a narrow speaking space between the portion marks, and the records shelf remains visible from the table’s end.
scenes.adaptation: Use local tables and dishes under the death-faith overlay. The chamber need not be an Icecrown crypt or undead-only institution; sizing and seating follow actual inhabitants.

10.label: Sargerism
10.nativeMeaning: Sargerism serves the Dark Titan’s annihilating crusade and its fel demonic army. Its venue should communicate cruelty, submission and life reduced to expendable fuel through the environment; it should not overwrite an individual character’s personality.
10.sourceDecision: A small annihilation altar and cult command niche can travel with Legion worship. Faith presence establishes the cultic setting, while actual portals, demons, victims and soul engines remain separately evidenced.

scenes.label: The Dark Titan’s Altar of Submission
scenes.availability: the locality follows Sargerism. Local cult shrine, appropriated hall or sheltered Legion devotional compound in a Sargerist locality. Use a small altar and ordinary ritual implements. Live captives, sacrifice, captured souls, demons and open portals require actual current events or participants, rather than county faith alone.
scenes.art: Make a horned, angular image of the Dark Titan dominate a black altar slab. Iron restraint fittings, an ash basin and sealed ritual vessels frame its lower surface. Acid-green glass lamps throw hard color onto knife-like Legion marks, with crimson cloth and scorched material adding a sense of consumed life. A side command niche holds campaign diagrams and tally surfaces, while a narrow approach exposes arrivals to the central image. Keep local architecture beneath the severe conversion overlay. No portal, living captive or demonic audience occupies the scene; its menace comes from worship organized around submission, extraction and the reduction of worlds to ash.
contexts: The horned image rises above a black slab fitted with iron restraints. An ash basin and sealed vessels stand beneath harsh green lamplight, beside angular marks cut across the older walls. Campaign diagrams occupy a side niche where the altar remains in view. Sargerists dedicate this place to the Dark Titan’s burning crusade, giving the extinguishment of life a devotional center. Visitors approach along the exposed central lane; the side niche provides a place for an order, a bargain or a challenge under that unrelenting image.
scenes.adaptation: Ordinary walls stay cultural and local, visibly overlaid or refitted with angular Legion marks. A village shrine can use a rough slab and painted icon; a rich center can use black iron and elaborate horned geometry.
scenes.purpose: Cult reception, orders, allegiance, negotiations and ritual preparation in a threatening religious setting.
scenes.lore: Native Sargerism establishes annihilation and demonic service. Blizzard’s warlock artifact history describes Sargeras empowering a soul-taking practitioner; Legion lore supports cultic corruption and soul bargains.
scenes.extrapolation: The local altar, restrained empty physical equipment and command niche are authored. The scene does not establish a current sacrifice, local soul engine or present Legion commander.

No portal, living captive or demonic audience occupies the scene; its menace comes from worship organized around submission, extraction and the reduction of worlds to ash.
Regional adaptation: Ordinary walls stay cultural and local, visibly overlaid or refitted with angular Legion marks. A village shrine can use a rough slab and painted icon; a rich center can use black iron and elaborate horned geometry.
Scene text: The horned image rises above a black slab fitted with iron restraints. An ash basin and sealed vessels stand beneath harsh green lamplight, beside angular marks cut across the older walls. Campaign diagrams occupy a side niche where the altar remains in view. Sargerists dedicate this place to the Dark Titan’s burning crusade, giving the extinguishment of life a devotional center. Visitors approach along the exposed central lane; the side niche provides a place for an order, a bargain or a challenge under that unrelenting image.
Use of the space: Cult reception, orders, allegiance, negotiations and ritual preparation in a threatening religious setting.
Lore basis: Native Sargerism establishes annihilation and demonic service. Blizzard’s warlock artifact history describes Sargeras empowering a soul-taking practitioner; Legion lore supports cultic corruption and soul bargains.
Extrapolation: The local altar, restrained empty physical equipment and command niche are authored. The scene does not establish a current sacrifice, local soul engine or present Legion commander.

10.label: Corruptism
10.nativeMeaning: Corruptism seeks unending power and control through fel contracts or demonic blood; GoA2 explicitly separates this from automatic Legion allegiance. Its space should display dangerous bargaining and appropriation of power rather than worshipful obedience to Sargeras.
10.sourceDecision: A covenant-and-power chamber can spread with the faith at modest scale. Vessels and binding marks preserve iconic fel practice without supplying pit-lord blood or a demon on every visit.

scenes.label: The Fel Covenant’s Power Chamber
scenes.availability: the locality follows Corruptism. Local warlock room, cult lodge or screened ritual work area in a Corruptist locality. Prepared circles, contract records and sealed empty vessels are sufficient. A current blood supply, pact negotiation with a real demon, soul expenditure or magical transformation requires actual context. The scene does not assert Legion allegiance.
scenes.art: Arrange a fel covenant chamber around a sharply inscribed binding circle and a bargaining table placed outside its boundary. Contract rolls, a horn-handled sealed vessel and empty shard settings lie beneath black-green cloth. Clamps, measuring tools and a heavy ritual knife make the pursuit of power practical and bodily. Green glass lamps cast jagged reflections across the ring while leaving the doorway readable. Retain local building and furniture craft, adding the dangerous ritual overlay without automatically importing orcish skull architecture. The circle waits between uses, with no present demon or flowing blood. Its geometry gives both summoner and petitioner positions while making the price of power visible.
contexts: Contract rolls lie outside the binding circle beside a sealed horn-handled vessel and empty shard settings. Green lamplight catches the sharp inscriptions and the clamps along the worktable. Corruptists seek power through bargains, blood and control, and covenant records gather their promises beside the ritual tools. A visitor can speak across the bargaining table while the circle remains clear beyond it. The vessel seals and worked inscriptions stay within reach of the seated negotiators, with the circle’s hard boundary visible between them and the invocation floor.
scenes.adaptation: Construction and ordinary instruments remain local; angular fel notation and black-green overlays carry the faith. Orcish tusks and clan hides are optional cultural variants, not required symbols for every convert.
scenes.purpose: Power bargains, warlock instruction, pact discussion and preparation for specifically current fel rites.
scenes.lore: Native Corruptism explicitly permits fel contracts and demon-blood power outside Legion allegiance. Blizzard’s Warcraft warlock preview establishes mastery of demons and soul-shard magic without inherent Legion service.
scenes.extrapolation: The portable covenant chamber, vessel design and worktable are authored. No universal blood-drinking liturgy, actual annihilan blood, occupied soul vessel or completed pact is assumed.

10.label: Alexstraszism
10.nativeMeaning: Reverence for the Red Flight makes protection of vulnerable life, empathy, justice and the sacred flame parts of one divine charge.
10.sourceDecision: A garden sanctuary with practical care space makes the native protection-of-life mission visible at an ordinary local scale.

scenes.label: The Life-Wardens’ Garden
scenes.availability: the locality follows Alexstraszism. A settled locality, courtyard or sheltered garden with maintained plants and clean water. Use a small planted refuge at modest scale; the faith venue implies ordinary upkeep, not a dragon nursery or actual Aspect.
scenes.art: Make a sheltered life garden whose unmistakable focus is a red dragon’s carved wings curving protectively around a broad stone or wooden care table. Scarlet and gold flowers stand among seedlings, clean water basins, folded linen, swaddling cloth and baskets of medicinal leaves. The wings are worked reliefs, suitable for local craftsmen, rather than living dragon limbs. Warm lamplight catches the red details and the pale bedding beneath a shade canopy. An open outer space receives travelers and petitioners; screened resting recesses allow practical care. Adapt the planting and roof to the climate, retaining the Red Flight’s generous, protective visual language at village or town scale.
contexts: Red dragon wings curve over the care table, carved in the same material as the garden’s shelter. Seedlings and scarlet flowers surround clean basins, swaddling cloth and medicinal leaves. Beneath the canopy, resting places look out toward the living beds. This sanctuary honors the Life-Binder’s charge through the protection of fragile life: a place for tending wounds, childbirth care, seeking shelter or asking help against an abuse of strength. The outer table admits visitors, while screens give those receiving care a little privacy. Water and warm leaves scent the sheltered air.
scenes.adaptation: Keep local architecture: dwarf stone planters, human timber colonnade, orc hide shade, arid pots or a winter conservatory. The red wing and care of living things are the common faith layer.
scenes.purpose: Care, sanctuary requests, protective vows and petitions about vulnerable people or creatures. Visitors use the outer garden; attendants manage the care recesses. Protected childbirth care is another use of the sanctuary, with no labor or infant automatically present.
scenes.lore: The native faith joins life, justice and compassion. Red Flight gardens and Alexstrasza’s ancient life-protection charge have canonical precedents. The native Sacred Childbirth tenet reinforces the protected birthing-care affordance.
scenes.extrapolation: Local mortal life-warden sanctuary, care equipment, red-wing shrine and visitor arrangements are authored adaptations; no universal named charitable order is asserted.

10.label: Yserism
10.nativeMeaning: The Green Flight’s divine charge is living balance and growth; its sacred Emerald Dream makes protected sleep a meaningful religious practice.
10.sourceDecision: A tended sleeping grove combines the native Dream connection with an accessible physical venue, without requiring a Dream portal.

scenes.label: The Sheltered Dreamer’s Grove
scenes.availability: the locality follows Yserism. A garden, wooded edge, planted courtyard or sheltered grove near habitation. Provide real shade, maintained plants and protected resting space. Dream entry or a dragon’s communication is an optional current event, not ambient scenery.
scenes.art: A green dragon relief stretches along the curved entrance of a protected sleeping grove. Broad leaves and a rootlike canopy shelter recessed pallets with green blankets, while a separate low watch platform faces the path. Shallow water bowls, seed trays and small carvings of local animals link the sanctuary’s rest to the living world around it. Use luminous leaf-filtered light, mossy greens and the intimate layered forms associated with the Green Flight. The plants remain ordinary local growth; no emerald portal fills the scene. Scale the shelter to the settlement and climate, keeping a clear distinction between the sleeping recesses and the place where awake visitors may gather.
contexts: A green dragon curves above the entrance, its carved tail following the grove’s sheltering roof. Blankets lie in recessed sleeping places among tended leaves and water bowls. The watch platform overlooks the approach, apart from the shaded pallets. Here, sleep is honored as a threshold toward the Emerald Dream, and the living garden embodies the balance its guardians protect. Visitors can wait with those keeping watch, leave a sleeper undisturbed or discuss troubling dreams. Leaves rustle above the recesses, carrying sound through the quiet court.
scenes.adaptation: Use native local trees or potted greenery; woven shade in desert towns, a conservatory in deep cold, or a planted stone recess underground. Local culture supplies the construction.
scenes.purpose: Dream discussions, watching over sleepers, nature counsel and a protected rest stop. Visitors gather on the waking side; entering another sleeper’s space needs permission.
scenes.lore: GoA2 explicitly gives Green Dragons a sacred Dream connection and communication through sleep. Canonical Green Flight groves and gardens supply the visual precedent.
scenes.extrapolation: A mortal neighborhood sleeping sanctuary and watch platform extrapolate those beliefs. Ordinary sleep neither grants Dream access nor produces prophetic messages.

10.label: Neltharism
10.nativeMeaning: The Black Flight’s original earth-warding charge sanctifies protection, order and the defense of Azeroth. Corruption is a danger within its history, not the faith’s default purpose.
10.sourceDecision: Earth-warding reliefs and a practical stone-and-forge court are plausible local expressions of this mission.

scenes.label: The Earth-Warder’s Stone Court
scenes.availability: the locality follows Neltharism. A settlement court, stoneworking yard or sheltered rock chamber. The ordinary local warding shrine can be small. Actual black-dragon presence, titan machinery or a corrupt cult variant requires its own current evidence.
scenes.art: Build a strong, low court around a dark dragon relief whose wings shelter a single rough stone taken from the surrounding land. An ordinary anvil, stoneworking tools and repaired defensive fittings occupy a side bay, making the Earth-Warder’s protection tangible. Heavy posts or compact arches give the space grounded weight; black scale patterns, bronze straps and red forge embers supply the flight’s palette. Leave a broad central floor before the stone for vows, petitions and instruction. Materials follow the local builders, from dwarf-cut masonry to rough orc stone and timber. The centerpiece is a local emblem of stewardship, not a magically active Dragon Isles oathstone.
contexts: The dark dragon relief spreads its wings over a rough local stone. An anvil and stoneworking tools stand beneath the side shelter, close to repaired hinges, shield rims and defensive fittings. The central floor remains clear before the shrine. Its imagery recalls the Earth-Warder’s charge to protect Azeroth and keep destructive forces in check. A petition, promise of defense or discussion of threatened ground can take place within sight of the stone. The workshop edge offers a less formal place to talk, with iron, dust and hearth smoke in the air.
scenes.adaptation: Use local stone and metals, retaining the black wing silhouette and protective earth imagery; timber settlements may mount the relief above a masonry hearth. Avoid copying a dragon-sized citadel.
scenes.purpose: Defense petitions, stewardship vows, boundary concerns and practical conversations with craftspeople. The open shrine court receives visitors; working tools belong to the attendants.
scenes.lore: Native Neltharism emphasizes safeguarding earth, order and balance. The canonical Black Flight’s forge and mining spaces support the practical materials motif.
scenes.extrapolation: Local earth-stone shrine and warding workshop are authored faith adaptations. Their exact furnishings are not an established universal Black Flight liturgy.

10.label: Malygosism
10.nativeMeaning: The Blue Flight’s divine mission is understanding, responsible use and preservation of Azeroth’s magic, including the cataloging of knowledge.
10.sourceDecision: A small arcane archive provides the faith a useful portable venue, preserving scholarship as sacred stewardship rather than requiring a Nexus.

scenes.label: The Spell-Keepers’ Archive
scenes.availability: the locality follows Malygosism. A settlement shrine-room, library alcove or sheltered teaching court. Scale from a single guarded book chest and instruction table to a larger archive. Magical wards or demonstrations may occur when actually active; no ley-line convergence is required.
scenes.art: Compose an arcane shrine-library with a blue dragon clasp above a central instruction desk. Books, scroll tubes and inscribed local tablets stand in orderly shelves or locked chests, with spiral spell diagrams displayed on a teaching board. Deep sapphire cloth, silver fittings and cool blue lamps give the archive its flight identity. A visitor table sits outside the railing that protects the records, while a cleared demonstration circle is drawn beside the desk. Retain the local culture’s roof, script and furniture. The space should suggest serious magical stewardship and beautifully intricate study, without filling an ordinary village with floating Nexus architecture or permanent spectacular spell effects.
contexts: The blue dragon clasp hangs over an instruction desk covered with careful spell diagrams. Scroll tubes, books and inscribed tablets occupy the shelves behind a low railing. Visitors have a table on the outer side, within view of the cleared demonstration circle. This archive treats knowledge and the responsible handling of magic as sacred duties of the Blue Flight. A spell can be discussed, a record requested or a disputed discovery examined with its keeper. Cool lamplight catches silver fittings, and the close room smells of ink, binding leather and polished wood.
scenes.adaptation: Keep the local alphabet, furniture and building traditions; blue dragon imagery and careful separation of records from visitor space identify the faith. Ice or floating towers belong only to suitable local backgrounds.
scenes.purpose: Spell research, access negotiations, teaching, examination of magical claims and disputed ownership of knowledge. Public discussion is welcome at the outer table; records are handled with the keeper’s permission.
scenes.lore: The native description makes magical understanding, responsibility and cataloging central. Canonical Blue Flight public libraries and Azure Archives provide concrete venue precedents.
scenes.extrapolation: A mortal local archive with permission boundaries is an authored adaptation, not a claim that all followers possess blue-dragon expertise or access to the Nexus.

10.label: Nozdormism
10.nativeMeaning: The Bronze Flight preserves time and causality. Mortal followers interpret its inscrutable mission through fate, predestination and the value of keeping an unbroken account.
10.sourceDecision: A timekeeping memorial court offers physical faith imagery and social use without presuming time travel or a temporal anomaly.

scenes.label: The Bronze Hourglass Court
scenes.availability: the locality follows Nozdormism. A settlement shrine court, record room or sheltered memorial space. Use ordinary clocks, hourglasses and records. A real timeway, temporal vision or visiting Bronze Dragon is a separate current event.
scenes.art: Center a mortal-scale faith court on an elegant bronze hourglass held between two curling dragon forms. A sundial or water clock stands nearby, with dated tablets, family records and memorial ribbons arranged along a low wall. Sand-colored cloth and warm metallic reflections evoke the Bronze Flight without forcing a desert backdrop. Leave a central reading space and a sheltered archivist’s table so the place works for remembrance, consultation and talk about omens or destiny. Adapt clocks and records to the local culture and weather. The hourglass remains a physical emblem: no time threads, historical apparitions or impossible duplicate people appear around it.
contexts: Sand falls through the bronze-framed hourglass between curling dragon forms. Dated tablets and memorial ribbons follow the court’s low wall, while records lie on the sheltered keeper’s table. The faith remembers the Bronze Flight’s charge to preserve time, even when its mortal followers can understand little of that vast work. Visitors may mark a death, compare an old account or ask what an omen means for a life thought to be fated. The measured clock and clear central floor leave room for conversation beneath the warm metalwork.
scenes.adaptation: Use local bronze work or bronze-colored fittings and regional script; a covered water clock may replace an exposed sundial in dark or wet settings. No Tanaris cavern or giant time machinery is needed.
scenes.purpose: Remembrance, genealogical claims, interpreting omens, discussing destiny and consulting historical records. The court is open; keepers supervise archive access.
scenes.lore: The native description distinguishes cosmic time stewardship from mortal belief in predestination. Canonical Bronze hourglass imagery and Timewalker scholarship support the material motifs.
scenes.extrapolation: Neighborhood memorial court, chronological tablets and local mortal record-keeping are plausible spatial extrapolation. The shrine itself has no temporal power.

10.label: Goldrinnism
10.nativeMeaning: Goldrinnists honor the Great Wolf and seek to awaken the beast within. Their devotion embraces instinct, fury and feral strength.
10.sourceDecision: A wolf shrine with a rough proving floor gives that unusually bodily faith a portable social place without making the worgen curse universal.

scenes.label: The Great Wolf’s Proving Ground
scenes.availability: the locality follows Goldrinnism. A settlement edge, hunting lodge court or sheltered outdoor practice ground. A modest wolf carving and practice floor are sufficient. Transformation, cursed initiation or a real manifestation of Goldrinn needs an active scene event. Blood Feast fixtures reflect the native tenet; an actual sentient sacrifice or consumption requires a current selected rite and participants.
scenes.art: A powerful white or pale wolf effigy overlooks a rough proving floor, its carved mane swept back and jaws lifted in a fierce open howl. Paw marks run along low boundary stones; claw-scored timber posts and weighted practice shields show a place used bodily rather than a polite ornamental chapel. Hides shelter an outer gathering ledge, with a fire, blood-catching offering slab and feast bowls beneath the wolf’s gaze. Use rugged textures, strong shoulders and a moon-pale animal silhouette. The local culture determines construction and weapons. Keep the ground accessible for demonstrations, challenges and talk; no compulsory transformed worgen or living god stands in the center.
contexts: The pale wolf effigy raises its jaws over the proving floor. Paw-marked stones and scored practice posts frame the ground; hides shelter a fire, blood-catching slab and feast bowls. Goldrinn’s shrine celebrates the beast within: instinct, ferocity and the strength taken through the sacred blood feast are part of its devotion. A visitor can watch training, discuss a hunt or accept a challenge if one is offered. The outer ledge provides room for a quieter exchange while the broad floor remains visible beneath the wolf’s carved mane.
scenes.adaptation: Followers of any culture can build the wolf effigy from their own stone, wood or worked metal. Local hides, paths and climate replace Hyjal’s conifers; the feral animal silhouette stays dominant.
scenes.purpose: Training, chosen challenges, hunt stories, arguments about restraint and feral power. Spectators remain on the outer ledge; participation is voluntary and separately selected.
scenes.lore: Native Goldrinnism seeks awakening of the beast within. Goldrinn’s canonical shrine and druidic pack form establish strong wolf/fury imagery, while the pack form’s history warns against assuming safe universal transformation. GoA2 adds Blood Feast and Natural Primitivism: blood offered to the divine and flesh consumed for the deceased’s wisdom and strength.
scenes.extrapolation: A local proving ground, practice gear and pale wolf image are authored adaptations of the faith. The scene neither confers a curse nor turns every adherent into a druid. Passive feast equipment makes that native rite legible; no sacrificial victim or compelled feast is present.

Regional adaptation: Followers of any culture can build the wolf effigy from their own stone, wood or worked metal. Local hides, paths and climate replace Hyjal’s conifers; the feral animal silhouette stays dominant.
Scene text: The pale wolf effigy raises its jaws over the proving floor. Paw-marked stones and scored practice posts frame the ground; hides shelter a fire, blood-catching slab and feast bowls. Goldrinn’s shrine celebrates the beast within: instinct, ferocity and the strength taken through the sacred blood feast are part of its devotion. A visitor can watch training, discuss a hunt or accept a challenge if one is offered. The outer ledge provides room for a quieter exchange while the broad floor remains visible beneath the wolf’s carved mane.
Use of the space: Training, chosen challenges, hunt stories, arguments about restraint and feral power. Spectators remain on the outer ledge; participation is voluntary and separately selected.
Lore basis: Native Goldrinnism seeks awakening of the beast within. Goldrinn’s canonical shrine and druidic pack form establish strong wolf/fury imagery, while the pack form’s history warns against assuming safe universal transformation. GoA2 adds Blood Feast and Natural Primitivism: blood offered to the divine and flesh consumed for the deceased’s wisdom and strength.
Extrapolation: A local proving ground, practice gear and pale wolf image are authored adaptations of the faith. The scene neither confers a curse nor turns every adherent into a druid. Passive feast equipment makes that native rite legible; no sacrificial victim or compelled feast is present.

10.label: Ursinism
10.nativeMeaning: The bear twins embody complementary paths: Ursol’s nature wisdom and shamanic/druidic magic, and Ursoc’s fierce strength in hunting and war.
10.sourceDecision: A paired shrine and a separate practice ground preserve both halves of the native faith, with different opportunities for roleplay.

scenes.label: The Twin Bears’ Council Hearth
scenes.availability: the locality follows Ursinism. A settlement shrine, lodge, sheltered grove or rock chamber. Small paired bear carvings suffice. No actual Ancient, ancestral ghost, Ursoc relic or living bear is required.
scenes.art: Two bear forms flank a broad council hearth. Ursol’s side has flowing branch knots, a carved staff and bowls of medicinal leaves; Ursoc’s has heavy claw grooves, hunter’s shields and blunt strength-training stones. The shared hearth and offering shelf unite the two paths rather than placing one above the other. Guest blankets, covered food bowls, amber lamps and earth-colored surfaces make the gathering space warm, weighty and intimate. A clear visitor approach reaches the hearth while a quieter side recess shelters teaching or counsel. Adapt the carving and room to local builders, retaining the paired powerful bear silhouettes instead of requiring a replica of Timbermaw Hold.
contexts: Two carved bears face the shared hearth. Branch knots and a staff mark Ursol’s side; claw grooves and heavy shields mark Ursoc’s. Bowls of leaves and hunters’ offerings meet on the same shelf, with guest blankets and covered food at the hearth. The sanctuary holds the twins’ complementary paths together: nature’s wisdom beside the strength that defends it. Visitors can seek counsel, bring an offering or hear how a hunt or conflict should serve the balance of the wild. Firelight reaches the broad gathering floor, while a side recess shelters closer teaching beneath the bears’ carved shoulders.
scenes.adaptation: Use local joinery, stone carving and textiles; northern furbolg timber is a strong reference but the faith remains legible in a dwarf stone lodge or human woodland hall.
scenes.purpose: Counsel, offerings, mediation between martial and nature-focused adherents, teaching and communal remembrance. Visitors approach the common hearth; private teaching uses the side recess. Guest reception, a meal and sheltered rest express the faith’s ritual hospitality.
scenes.lore: The native faith explicitly divides Ursol’s and Ursoc’s paths. Canonical furbolg devotion and Timbermaw’s twin-bear shrine provide precedent for paired sacred forms. The native Ritual Hospitality tenet supports receiving guests with food and sheltered rest.
scenes.extrapolation: Local council hearth, symbolic side furnishings and seating are authored portable arrangements. No living twin or unique titansteel claw relic is assumed.

scenes.label: The Bear’s Trial Circle
scenes.availability: the locality follows Ursinism. A settlement practice ground, lodge yard or sheltered exercise court. Use ordinary physical practice equipment. An organized trial is optional; spirits, magical transformations and direct divine trials require current events.
scenes.art: Lay out a broad earth or sand practice circle bordered by bear-paw stones. Heavy lifting blocks, padded wooden shields and scarred wrestling posts emphasize Ursoc’s bodily strength; a side lane with staffs and carefully set stepping stones gives Ursol’s discipline and judgment equal presence. Twin bear emblems face the ground from a modest shrine post. Hide shade or a sturdy local roof shelters the observers’ side, leaving clear lanes for movement. Use tough natural textures and practical wear instead of a ceremonial arena’s excessive grandeur. The space suits voluntary instruction and tests of strength, endurance or cooperation without a spirit bear materializing as judge.
contexts: Bear-paw stones border the broad practice floor. Lifting blocks and worn wrestling posts occupy one side; staffs and a measured line of stepping stones occupy the other. The twin bears watch from carvings above the observer shelter. Here, strength is practiced alongside discipline and judgment, reflecting Ursoc’s fierce path and Ursol’s guiding wisdom. Company can gather under the shelter to discuss a hunter’s readiness, arrange instruction or watch a chosen trial. The floor’s scuff marks show repeated effort, with a clear approach between the heavier training stones.
scenes.adaptation: Select local stones, wood, hides and weapons; leave floor and equipment broad enough for the actual participants’ bodies. Snow, desert or city surroundings alter the shelter, not the paired strength/wisdom purpose.
scenes.purpose: Voluntary practice, instruction, judging readiness, chosen trials and friendly or serious competition. Spectators use the sheltered edge; the engine does not force a challenge.
scenes.lore: Native Ursinism joins warrior/hunter ferocity with nature wisdom. The canonical Trials of Ursol ask for strength, courage and the ability to apply oneself effectively.
scenes.extrapolation: A local physical practice yard inspired by those values is extrapolated. It does not reproduce Ursol’s unique direct divine trial or add a universal formal rite.

10.label: Elunism
10.nativeMeaning: Elune leads a pantheon honored by authoritative priestesses and nature-protecting druids. Devotion joins moonlit care, the Ancient Guardians and remembrance of ancestral sacrifice.
10.sourceDecision: Moonwells are the strongest documented portable example; a local priestess sanctuary gives a separate formal and ancestral setting without repeating a unique temple.

scenes.label: The Local Moonwell
scenes.availability: the locality follows Elunism. A settled locality with a maintained water basin, shrine court or sheltered garden. County faith makes an ordinary plausible local moonwell available. Fit the water basin to settlement resources; arid locations use maintained or transported water. Consecration draws on existing blessed waters and ordinary faith practice; it creates no global Well of Eternity or guaranteed cure.
scenes.art: Place a modest moonwell at the heart of a local shrine court, its clear consecrated water giving a soft silver-blue glow against a crescent-carved rim. A dry receiving edge holds clean bowls, folded cloth and small offerings of flowers or food; a shaded resting place lies beside it. Preserve the iconic pool, lunar carving and reflected cool light as the reusable overlay. Let local builders determine the surrounding masonry, timber, metalwork or living wood, and let the biome determine the plants and shelter. A desert court may shelter a carefully maintained cistern rather than an abundant spring. The scene’s ordinary scale makes Elune’s sacred water a practical presence in local life.
contexts: The moonwell’s clear water casts silver-blue light across its crescent rim. Clean bowls, folded cloth and small offerings rest on the dry edge, beside a sheltered place to sit. Consecrated waters connect this local shrine to the older wells honored by Elune’s followers. Priestesses may bless provisions, tend the weary or prepare water for sacred use here; visitors can ask for care, leave an offering or speak beside the pool. The surrounding materials belong to the local builders, while the reflected lunar glow gives the court its familiar sacred heart.
scenes.adaptation: The faith supplies the moonwell, not a mandatory night-elf town. Use dwarf-cut cistern stone, human courtyard masonry, orc timber-and-stone enclosure or local living wood; desert shade, winter shelter and ordinary native plants adapt the setting.
scenes.purpose: Rest, care requests, provision blessing, offerings, meditation and conversations with a local attendant. Visitors remain on the dry receiving edge unless invited into ritual work; actual blessings and cures follow current participants and events.
scenes.lore: Moonwells are repeatedly documented as settlement and temple shrines with practical sacred uses. The founding ritual demonstrates transported consecrated water and offerings rather than requiring every new site to be beside an original cosmic well.
scenes.extrapolation: Cross-cultural basin design, ordinary new-convert establishment and climate adaptation are portable extrapolation. Its visible sacred water does not guarantee a miracle or imply unrestricted secular bathing.

scenes.label: The Moon Priestess’s Sanctuary
scenes.availability: the locality follows Elunism. A settlement shrine-room, covered sacred court or modest temple. A small local sanctuary is sufficient. The officiant follows the active faith’s actual social doctrine; named high priestesses, historic statues and Night Warrior rites are separate current elements.
scenes.art: Create a modest sanctuary around a silver lunar disc above a crescent altar. Pale cloth, small lamps, bowls of leaves and memorial offerings give the room a moonlit sacred rhythm; a roof opening or side arch faces the sky where the climate allows. A receiving place near the altar makes the priestess’s public authority legible, while a screened side space holds clean water vessels, shrouds and ceremonial linen. Local materials shape the hall, retaining strong lunar ornament and the balance of compassionate care with solemn ancestral remembrance. Keep the foreground open for audiences and offerings rather than furnishing it as a ruler’s throne room.
contexts: A silver lunar disc hangs above the crescent altar. Lamps brighten pale cloth, bowls of leaves and memorial offerings arranged beneath it. The priestess’s receiving place faces the open floor, with clean vessels and folded ceremonial linen screened to one side. The sanctuary joins Elune’s care for the living with honor for those whose sacrifices protect them. A visitor may present a petition, arrange a blessing or speak about remembrance and burial. The side screen shelters preparation, while lamplight catches the lunar disc above the altar.
scenes.adaptation: Keep the local construction language and bodily scale. Silver-blue cloth, crescents, moon-facing opening where practical and nature/ancestor offerings carry the faith; no mandatory Darnassus replica or specific Haidene image.
scenes.purpose: Faith counsel, petitions to religious authority, blessings, memorial arrangements and burial discussions. Visitors use the receiving floor; ceremonial preparation belongs to the officiants and those invited.
scenes.lore: The native faith gives the Sisters substantial authority and honors ancestral sacrifice. Canonical priestesses staff temples and chapterhouses, give counsel/care, and cleanse the dead with moonlit water.
scenes.extrapolation: A portable small sanctuary, receiving floor and screened preparation bay are authored spatial arrangements. Named temple institutions and a mandatory funeral in progress are excluded.

10.label: Agamagganism
10.nativeMeaning: Shamans and geomancers invoke Agamaggan, the immense Great Boar, for bodily strength in battle and sacred rituals.
10.sourceDecision: A tusk-and-briar invocation court is portable; blood shards remain special objects rather than automatically occurring under every converted settlement.

scenes.label: The Great Boar’s Briar Court
scenes.availability: the locality follows Agamagganism. A local outdoor shrine, thorn enclosure or sheltered earthen court. Use locally grown, cultivated or woven thorn forms and a carved boar image. Actual blood shards, ancestral divine thorns and Agamaggan’s original remains are separate current possessions or locations. Actual sentient sacrifice or consumption needs a selected current Blood Feast rite; vessels and the slab are passive venue equipment.
scenes.art: A broad, blunt boar face dominates an earthen shrine, with outward-curving tusk uprights and hooked briar screens enclosing the open invocation floor. Blood-catching stone bowls, drums, feast vessels and a geomancer’s slab give the space forceful practical use. Ordinary red-stained pebbles or carved stone offerings carry the Great Boar’s blood-and-earth symbolism without masquerading as authentic blood shards. Make the altar squat, powerful and physically heavy, its carved bristles echoed by pointed fencework. Local builders supply the material language and shelter. Thorn planting, woven branches or sculpted briars can carry the same motif across different climates, leaving broad gaps for company to gather before the tusks.
contexts: The Great Boar’s carved face fills the low shrine between sweeping tusks. Hooked briars enclose an open earthen floor, with drums, blood-catching bowls and feast vessels beside the geomancer’s slab. Red-stained stone offerings recall the blood and strength associated with Agamaggan’s sacrifice. Battle invocations and earth rites share the court with the Blood Feast: blood offered to the divine, flesh taken for strength and wisdom. The broad entrance admits company, while the briar screens shelter those working beside the slab. Dust, worked stone and dry branches scent the court.
scenes.adaptation: Any adopting culture can render the boar in local wood, stone or metal. Thorns may be physical thorn planting or carved/woven briar forms in hostile climates; avoid instantly reproducing Razorfen’s divine giant growth.
scenes.purpose: Battle preparations, shamanic consultation, offerings and discussion of sacred earth or desired strength. The outer floor receives visitors; ritual tools are handled by their keepers.

Canonical Agamaggan devotion connects thorns and blood shards with the Great Boar’s sacrifice and gifts of strength. Native Blood Feast explicitly gives sentient sacrifice and ritual flesh consumption. Consolamentum is also present in native declarations, without inventing an Agamaggan-specific canonical liturgy for it.
scenes.extrapolation: A local invocation court, red-stained non-relic offerings and adaptable ordinary briar screen are extrapolated; no new blood shards or divine thorn growth is generated.

10.label: Vindicatorism
10.nativeMeaning: Vindicatorism treats fel power and even cruel sacrifice as tools for defeating evil. Its followers justify dangerous means through a purpose greater than personal gain.
10.sourceDecision: A guarded fel training-and-containment court plausibly accompanies this faith without identifying every devotee as Illidari or making demon-soul consumption universal.

scenes.label: The Vigil of the Borrowed Flame
scenes.availability: the locality follows Vindicatorism. A settled stronghold courtyard, fortified shrine-room or defended training shelter. The local faith venue needs ordinary containment equipment and controlled access. Actual demons, fel transformations, soul consumption or sacrifice occur only in a selected current event.
scenes.art: Build a grim defended court whose green-lit lamps illuminate inward-facing binding marks around a scarred practice floor. Demon-emblem targets, damaged armor and sealed reagent chests show fel power being studied as a weapon against its own masters. A substantial barrier separates the visitor shelf from the marked work area; warning carvings and a disciplined equipment layout keep the danger visible. Use local masonry, timber or metal, carrying fel-green details as the portable religious layer. The mood is severe and sacrificial rather than gleeful demon worship. Keep the circles unoccupied by summoned creatures and give the outer shelf room for a guarded negotiation or request for aid.
contexts: Green lamps light the binding marks around the scarred practice floor. Demon-emblem targets stand beside damaged armor and sealed reagent chests, behind a substantial barrier. The court is devoted to using fel power against the evils that wield it, with the costs of that choice visible in its worn equipment. Visitors speak from the outer shelf, where the marked floor remains in view. A request for aid, an argument about acceptable sacrifice or a discussion of dangerous training can unfold here without crossing into the working circle.
scenes.adaptation: Use the culture’s own fortification and weapon forms; maintain the green fel motif, outward defense purpose and restrained inside/outside access. No compulsory blindfolds, horns or elf-only institution.
scenes.purpose: Aid negotiations, arguments about necessary sacrifice, dangerous training discussions and guarded cooperation. Outsiders use the visitor shelf; the marked work area requires admission.
scenes.lore: Native Vindicatorism supplies the ends-and-means theology. Canonical Illidari use their enemies’ power against the Legion, accept sacrifice and train in guarded demonic settings, providing a related visual precedent.
scenes.extrapolation: The local vigil court is an authored institution, not an asserted canonical universal Vindicator order or equivalence to the Illidari. No personal demon-hunter transformation is implied.
