10.label: Black Harvest
10.nativeMeaning: The Black Harvest shares stolen and discovered magical power through collaboration while seeking mastery over demons. Its severe internal discipline casts out weakness and betrayal.
10.sourceDecision: A local coven exchange room with a controlled binding floor captures collaboration and dangerous mastery, rather than default Legion submission.

scenes.label: The Coven’s Exchange Circle
scenes.availability: the locality follows Black Harvest. A local coven room, controlled shrine chamber or guarded basement. County faith permits a local circle of adherents without spawning the named founding council or Dreadscar Rift. Exceptional summons and soul punishments require current actions.
scenes.art: Arrange a dark coven chamber around a communal table, with research desks facing inward so discoveries can be compared rather than hoarded in separate cells. Green lamps catch sealed reagent jars, closed shard containers and heavily annotated grimoires. Beyond a low barrier lies an empty binding circle, its marks repeatedly repaired after hard use. A screened outer alcove receives applicants, patrons or uneasy allies without giving them free access to the coven’s work. Local architecture supplies the room’s shell; fel-green light, controlled dangerous tools and the inward-facing study arrangement supply the faith identity. The place should feel powerful, competitive and exacting, with no named councilors or mandatory summoned demon.
contexts: The coven’s desks face a shared table beneath green lamps. Annotated grimoires, sealed jars and closed shard containers stand within reach of the scholars’ side. An empty binding circle occupies the floor beyond a low barrier, its repaired lines showing repeated use. The Black Harvest’s pursuit of power takes a collaborative but unforgiving form here: discoveries can be shared, bargains examined and candidates tested against the coven’s standards. Visitors wait in the screened outer alcove. Ink, hot wax and sharp reagents scent the chamber, while the open table keeps fellow members in each other’s view.

10.label: Gogism
10.nativeMeaning: Gogism honors Gorgog’s defeat of the gronn and the proof that supposed gods could be broken. Arcane mastery is an honored path associated with that victorious imperial legacy.
10.sourceDecision: A founder’s victory hall with arcane teaching is a plausible portable expression, using carved trophies where original gronn remains are unavailable.

scenes.label: The Gronnslayer’s Victory Hall
scenes.availability: the locality follows Gogism. A settled shrine hall, teaching court or broad local assembly shelter. Use crafted images of gronn remains, scaled to the actual local population. Genuine giant trophies or Apexis artifacts require present possession; neither is automatic. The native Ritual Cannibalism tenet justifies feast fixtures; an actual meal of sentient flesh requires current material and chosen participants.
scenes.art: Give the hall an assertive triumphal focus: a founder relief stands beneath a carved frame of cracked giant ribs, with a deep bowl emblem recalling the marrow by which Gorgog disproved his enemies’ divinity. The bone forms are visibly carved substitutes unless actual trophies exist. An elevated instruction platform and arcane diagrams honor magecraft beside the victory display. Broad pillars, strong horizontal lines and polished local stone or timber evoke the confidence of the Gorian legacy without copying its palace. Leave a large assembly floor, petitioners’ edge and heavy feast table with ritual serving bowls. The room should communicate hard-won mastery, imperial ambition and proud magical learning rather than generic shamanic totems.
contexts: Carved giant ribs frame the founder’s relief above a deep bowl emblem. The cracked forms recall Gorgog’s proof that the gronn could be broken and their supposed divinity stripped away. An instruction platform carries arcane diagrams beside a heavy feast table and ritual serving bowls. Victory, magecraft and ritual consumption have places in the same hall, where power and authority can be displayed or disputed. Petitioners can wait along the side pillars within sight of both the founder’s image and the teaching place. Polished surfaces carry voices across the broad floor.
scenes.adaptation: Keep broad victorious silhouettes but scale seats and doorways for the adopting culture. Native ogre monumental forms inspire the motif; a human hall or dwarf chamber need not become an ogre-sized palace.
scenes.purpose: Victory claims, magical demonstrations when chosen, teaching, petitions and debate about power or legitimate authority. Visitors use the assembly floor and petitioner edge; instruction follows actual teachers.
scenes.lore: The native description explicitly connects the founder’s gronn destruction and marrow consumption with honored arcane magic. Chronicle-derived lore describes displaying defeated gronn skeletons and building an immense hall. The native faith adds Ritual Cannibalism and Hedonism, reinforcing the feast table alongside honored magecraft.
scenes.extrapolation: Local commemorative victory hall, carved replacement bones and teaching platform are extrapolated. No canonically established universal Gogic temple or literal gronn trophy supply is asserted.

10.label: Ragnarism
10.nativeMeaning: Ragnarists revere and fear the Firelord’s destructive, purifying flame, submitting through his intercessor and seeking a merciless master’s favor.
10.sourceDecision: A maintained furnace altar expresses flame submission at portable scale without a lava sea or a summoned Ragnaros.

scenes.label: The Firelord’s Furnace Altar
scenes.availability: the locality follows Ragnarism. A local fireproof shrine room, forge court or stone-lined outdoor enclosure. A maintained ordinary furnace or brazier is sufficient. Fit ventilation and fuel to the place. Ragnaros, flamewakers, molten portals and catastrophic fire are distinct current events.
scenes.art: Make the furnace mouth the court’s commanding sacred focus, its fierce orange light rising beneath a heavy hammer-and-flame relief. An ash-black offering ledge fronts the fire, with scorched chains, iron bowls and charred devotional remnants arranged along the stone. A raised officiant’s place stands to one side, giving intercession a severe public shape. Black metal, red-hot ember color and monumental squat geometry carry the Firelord’s visual language at a scale a local settlement can maintain. Provide a marked outer receiving edge beyond the furnace’s heat. Use a ventilated fireproof room or lined outdoor court, without requiring lava, elemental servants or the Firelord’s actual body.
contexts: The furnace throws orange light beneath the hammer-and-flame relief. Ash coats the offering ledge, where iron bowls and charred devotional remnants lie beside scorched chains. The officiant’s raised place overlooks the cleared floor and the outer receiving edge. This shrine approaches the Firelord through fear, submission and the promise of purification by flame. Visitors can present an offering, request intercession or negotiate with those who keep the furnace. Heat presses against the inner floor, while the marked edge gives company a place to stand beyond its fiercest reach.
scenes.adaptation: Use local fireproof stone, clay or metal and available fuel; surface settlements can use a lined fire court. Dark Iron angular ironwork is a motif reference, not a mandatory culture or volcanic landscape.
scenes.purpose: Offerings, intercession requests, negotiations with fire clergy and discussions of submission or purification. Visitors remain on the outer edge; furnace work and rites require invitation.
scenes.lore: The native faith supplies destructive purification and merciless intercession. Canonical Ragnaros worship and Dark Iron labor under the Firelord give the furnace/forge motif concrete context.
scenes.extrapolation: A local furnace altar and officiant platform are authored portable forms. No named Majordomo, forced sacrifice or limitless supernatural fuel is generated.

10.label: Ordonism
10.nativeMeaning: Ordon devotion honors Ordos’s agonizing fiery ascension. Fire-keepers emulate his burning sacrifice and offer prayers or enchantments to ease his endless pain.
10.sourceDecision: A fire-keeper’s ember court makes this particular pain-and-ascension devotion distinct from generic fire worship; self-immolation belongs to an optional active rite.

scenes.label: The Fire-Keepers’ Ember Vigil
scenes.availability: the locality follows Ordonism. A fireproof local shrine court or sheltered stone/clay enclosure. Maintain a normal ritual fire and safe outer receiving space. An actual self-immolation rite, active pain-easing enchantment or divine appearance needs a present participant/event.
scenes.art: Center the court on a deeply worked image of Ordos, his horned form wrapped in carved flames and an unmistakable posture of suffering. A broad ritual brazier faces the image, with an ash-dark inner circle and a side shelf holding covered oil vessels, censers and rows of heavy candles. The strong contrast between glowing embers and blackened stone conveys devotion through pain and burning ascension. A dry outer platform leaves room for prayer, waiting and conversation beyond the hottest area. Build the shell in the adopting culture’s own fireproof materials. The deity remains an image and the ritual equipment remains ready, with no person automatically set alight.
contexts: The flame-wrapped image of Ordos faces a broad brazier. Ash darkens the inner circle, while covered oil vessels, censers and thick candles fill the preparation shelf. The fire-keepers’ devotion recalls a shaman’s ascent into divinity and the endless pain that followed it. Prayers for his relief and preparations to emulate that sacrifice belong here. Visitors can speak from the outer platform, arrange an offering or question the meaning of a costly vow. Ember heat reaches the edge in waves, with smoke drawn above the scorched circle.
scenes.adaptation: Local peoples retain their building forms. Ordos’s horned image is the depicted patron, not proof that all participants are yaungol. Adapt fuel, ventilation and weather shelter to each region.
scenes.purpose: Prayer, offerings, fire-keeper counsel and discussions of costly vows or the patron’s suffering. Visitors use the outer platform; preparations and chosen rites use the inner court.
scenes.lore: The native description closely follows Ordos’s in-game Adventure Guide: sacrifice to fire, endless agony, self-burning fire-keepers and prayers to ease pain. Ordon candlekeepers and firewatchers supply additional worship imagery.
scenes.extrapolation: A portable ember-vigil shrine, suffering carved image and preparation shelf are spatial extrapolation. Self-burning is a documented rite but does not happen automatically whenever this background is selected.

10.label: Krosi
10.nativeMeaning: Krosi worship treats the invisible sky-devilsaur as creator and physical devilsaurs as sacred kin. Its religious ideal is relentless growth, ferocity and strength.
10.sourceDecision: A devilsaur shrine joined to a rough hunt-feast and proving floor is portable without spawning a giant sacred beast in every new Krosi town.

scenes.label: The Sky-Devilsaur’s Hunt Court
scenes.availability: the locality follows Krosi. A local outdoor shrine, rough feast shelter or dry cave court. Use a carved devilsaur jaw and ordinary available hunting remains. A living sacred devilsaur, authentic giant trophy or the Echo of Kros appears only where actually present. Ritual Cannibalism is native faith practice; actual sentient remains, a flesh-taking rite or compelled participation are not part of the passive background.
scenes.art: A savage devilsaur jaw carving hangs above a heavy offering and meat-cutting slab. A tall stone beside it carries ascending claw marks and weapon notches, making continual growth and fighting strength visible. Ordinary hunting bones, coarse bowls and strips of meat occupy the slab and hooks beneath a rough shelter. Leave a broad proving floor in front and a dry observer ledge to one side. Use hard teeth silhouettes, rough ochre hides, smoke-dark surfaces and blunt, physical materials. The adopting culture supplies the building language; the sky-devilsaur and sacred predation supply the faith layer. No giant living dinosaur or immense imported fossil is required.
contexts: The devilsaur jaw carving bares its teeth above the heavy slab. Hunting bones and coarse bowls lie beneath it, beside strips of meat on the shelter’s hooks. Upward claw marks climb the tall stone at the floor’s edge. Kros is honored through growing strength and the taking of flesh; sacred cannibalism belongs to this faith’s predatory devotion. Company can bring a hunt’s offering, discuss a claim of strength or watch a chosen contest on the open ground. The dry ledge overlooks both the proving floor and the smoky feast shelter.
scenes.adaptation: Local builders can cut the jaw in stone, wood or metal; genuine devilsaur remains are optional. Keep the fierce predator motif and bodily devotional use, while local food, shelter and terrain vary.
scenes.purpose: Hunt offerings, strength claims, chosen contests, religious instruction and rough shared meals. Visitors can approach the observer ledge; handling offerings or taking part follows actual permission and choices.
scenes.lore: The native faith names Kros, sacred devilsaurs and continual fighting/growth. Skumblade saur-priest dialogue makes strength, meat and predation central to devotion; a live sacred devilsaur is documented only in particular places. GoA2 explicitly adds Ritual Cannibalism, so the flesh-taking affordance belongs to the faith rather than being merely a saurok racial custom.
scenes.extrapolation: A portable jaw image, marked proving stone and hunt-feast court are extrapolated. Skumblade’s local cultivated-filth policy is not made a universal rule for every adopting culture; sacred beasts and corpse consumption are not automatic.

10.label: Zan'atali
10.nativeMeaning: An ancient, adaptable Loa pantheon that recognizes other Loa and uses that openness to maintain ties between sects.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Court of Many Loa
scenes.availability: the locality follows Zan'atali. A public shrine court or settlement gathering space in a county following Zan’atali. Ordinary local shrine availability; select patron images appropriate to current worship. Sacred offices remain behind the offering rail.
scenes.art: A compact court gathers several Loa shrines around one shared approach. Give each niche a different beast silhouette—raptor jaw, winged face, horned head—rather than cloning the same idol. Bright cloth, feathers, offering bowls and shallow incense dishes animate sturdy carved forms. A low rail protects each sacred recess while a central paving strip and broad side seats receive petitioners, travelers and representatives of different sects. Use rich ochre, turquoise and vermilion accents on the host culture’s ordinary building material. This is a local meeting place, ranging from three village posts to a handsome town courtyard; its patrons are represented by crafted images.
contexts: Different Loa faces look down from adjoining shrines, each surrounded by its own colors and offerings. Incense settles beneath their brows, and bright cloth stirs over the shared approach. A visitor can place a gift at one rail without crossing another shrine’s sacred recess. Broad seats occupy the center, where local families, traveling devotees and envoys can compare claims or negotiate whose observance will take precedence. The court makes room for several loyalties in the same community; the arrangement of fresh offerings reveals which patrons currently command attention.
scenes.adaptation: Keep the local culture’s masonry or carpentry. Several niches are the religious constant; stone pyramids, golden capital architecture and tropical plants are optional local elaborations.
scenes.purpose: Offerings, inter-sect diplomacy, civic petitions and discussions of patronage have distinct public and sacred edges.
scenes.lore: GoA2 describes Zan’atali as adaptable and respectful of other Loa. Warcraft distinguishes personal, family, civic and national Loa worship and shows several shrines within a shared religious district.
scenes.extrapolation: The modest multi-shrine layout and common reception seating are portable spatial extrapolations; the scene does not copy Dazar’alor or appoint the actual Zanchuli Council.

10.label: Gur'atali
10.nativeMeaning: Death, Bwonsamdi and ancestors occupy a central place. The treatment of the dead includes ritual cannibalism in this mod’s native description.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Bwonsamdi’s Offering Shade
scenes.availability: the locality follows Gur'atali. A shrine beside the settlement’s funerary ground, ancestor hall or ordinary public religious court. Public outer apron; the keeper controls access to remains, offerings and the inner preparation area. No apparition is assumed.
scenes.art: Build a skull-faced shrine whose long, crooked horns and staring eye sockets dominate a shaded receiving apron. White bone, deep violet cloth, turquoise marks and red feathers contrast with the host culture’s timber or masonry. Ritual masks hang from a side beam; covered pots and a dark offering recess belong behind the sacred edge. Arrange a preparation stool to one side, with broader seating outside the shrine for relatives and petitioners. The atmosphere combines death’s intimacy with an unmistakably powerful, bargaining Loa: richly handmade, angular and unsettling. Let ordinary lamps catch crafted teeth and bone fittings; depict Bwonsamdi through the idol, not as a manifested character.
contexts: The skull-faced shrine grins above covered offering pots and a row of hanging masks. Bone fittings tap against one another in the sheltered air. A dark recess holds gifts set aside for Bwonsamdi, while family seats face the shrine from outside its sacred edge. Here the names of the dead, the handling of their remains and promises made to their keeper carry public weight. A petitioner can speak across the receiving mat; closer access to the vessels and preparation stool rests with whoever tends the shrine.
scenes.adaptation: A local sculptor can carve the same skull-faced motif into timber, stone or metal. Replace palm thatch with appropriate roofing and keep the burial setting suited to local practice.
scenes.purpose: Remembrance, funerary negotiations, ancestry and vows to the death Loa; outsiders can address the keeper from the outer apron.
scenes.lore: The mod explicitly centers Bwonsamdi and ancestral death observances. Warcraft shows masks, offerings and shrine-based petitions to Bwonsamdi.
scenes.extrapolation: A common local reception apron and covered memory vessels are authored fittings, distinct from the unique Necropolis or any actual bargain granting power.

scenes.label: Ancestral Feast House
scenes.availability: the locality follows Gur'atali. A local funerary preparation hall or protected room adjoining the community’s ancestral shrine. The room may be idle. A present body, actual funeral or consumption of remains must follow current scene circumstances rather than faith alone.
scenes.art: Create a solemn communal room with a heavy preparation slab behind a woven or carved screen and a long gathering table in front. Ancestor masks and remembrance vessels occupy the walls; broad serving bowls, clean knives, folded funerary cloth and a covered brazier make the ritual’s material requirements readable. Bone-white accents and muted blood-red binding distinguish this from an ordinary feast hall. Leave the slab clear and set no visible body or prepared human flesh in the baseline. Make the foreground usable for relatives disputing arrangements while the screen protects the preparation work. The host culture supplies the hall’s architecture, but the dead’s place in the meal gives its objects their specific significance.
contexts: Ancestor masks overlook a long table laid with broad bowls. Behind the screen, folded funerary cloth and clean knives wait beside an empty preparation slab. This community honors its dead through careful treatment of the body, and ritual consumption has a place among those observances. The covered vessels therefore carry a significance beyond ordinary hospitality. Relatives can settle the deceased’s wishes at the front table, while the screened room reserves the handling of remains for those entrusted with it. The hearth smells of warm spice and ash.

10.label: Drak'atali
10.nativeMeaning: The harsh-country Loa require strength of body and sharpness of mind; devotees pursue both throughout life.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Loa Trial Yard
scenes.availability: the locality follows Drak'atali. A settlement shrine yard with enough firm ground for instruction or local contests. Use existing weather and ground conditions. Ordinary practice is plausible; a formal trial, transformed champion or slaughtered Loa is a separate current event.
scenes.art: Place massive beast-faced shrine posts around a practical training yard: a rhino’s forward horn, a broad mammoth brow, a bear jaw and a watchful cat face give the Loa a heavy, forceful presence. Lifting stones, weighted beams and worn practice weapons share the sheltered edge with a carved board holding movable counters for instruction and problems. Use deep red bindings, pale teeth or crafted ivory-colored inlays, and strong angular patterns. Covered ritual feast bowls stand beneath the shrine. A clear observer strip lets a priest or visitor watch without entering the working floor. Keep the host culture’s architecture and the actual climate; a southern Drak’atali settlement carries its Loa images rather than an imported Northrend glacier.
contexts: Heavy beast faces overlook a yard worn smooth by repeated practice. Lifting stones and blunt training weapons stand near the shrine rail; under the shelter, carved counters lie beside a board used for problems and instruction. Drak’atali observance treats strength and a keen mind as related obligations to the Loa. The watching strip gives a teacher or challenger a clear view of the working ground, while the side bench allows quieter discussion of an error, a boast or a proposed test. Covered ritual feast bowls wait beneath the shrine. Scuffed grips and repaired bindings show the effort invested here.
scenes.adaptation: Adapt shelter and local materials to the occupied region. Snow and mammoth ivory are optional northern treatments, while the demanding beast silhouettes and combined intellectual/physical use travel with the faith.
scenes.purpose: Training, mentorship, claims to prowess, strategic disagreement and voluntary tests of capability.
scenes.lore: Native Drak’atali doctrine values bodily strength and intelligence. Drakkari worship several beast Loa and maintains distinct altars to them. Its native bloody feast tenet supports idle ceremonial meal fittings.
scenes.extrapolation: A combined local trial yard and problem board are honest extrapolations from the mod’s stated demands; no canon standardized riddle rite is asserted.

10.label: Am'atali
10.nativeMeaning: Hunting is sacred, the hunt’s Loa receive special reverence, and consuming a defeated opponent can hold greater honor than taking lesser prey.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Consecrated Hunt Yard
scenes.availability: the locality follows Am'atali. A settlement’s shrine-side hunt departure yard or return court. Public receiving edge; trophies reflect the locality and current circumstances. No captive, kill or ritual meal is generated automatically.
scenes.art: Frame a broad hunting yard with four powerful sacred silhouettes: lynx fangs, eagle wings, bear jaws and a sweeping dragonhawk crest. Prayer cords, amulets and vivid red cloth dress the shrine rail beside sharpened spears and inspected bows. A trophy beam bears local horn, hide and an old opponent’s decorated helm; a heavy bench with covered ceremonial bowls establishes the honored feast following the hunt. Give the scene feral dignity, predatory pride and extravagant beast masks rather than a quiet gamekeeper’s shed. Ordinary local builders supply the surrounding lodge or court. Separate the weapon and trophy floor from a clear outer approach where visitors can discuss a hunt without touching its consecrated fittings.
contexts: Lynx fangs and spread eagle wings crown the shrine above the hunting weapons. Amulets hang among the trophy mounts, and an opponent’s decorated helm sits beside horn and hide. The hunt here is a sacred undertaking: worthy prey can be a beast or an enemy, and the honored feast may include the defeated opponent. Covered bowls wait along the heavy bench. Visitors meet on the outer approach, where a proposed quarry, a disputed trophy or the terms of joining a hunt can be discussed before anyone enters the consecrated working yard.
scenes.adaptation: Keep the local architecture and available prey. Portable worship uses carved or painted Loa symbols; it need not create forest-troll trees, live bears or actual dragonhawks in every biome.
scenes.purpose: Arranging hunts, military boasting, interpreting trophies, negotiating access and debating the treatment of prey or enemies.
scenes.lore: GoA2 explicitly describes ritual hunting and consumption of worthy opponents. Amani Loa include Halazzi, Akil’zon, Nalorakk and Jan’alai; amulets and ceremonial beast masks appear in their veneration.
scenes.extrapolation: A local hunt departure/return court and its trophy arrangements are authored extrapolations. The scene does not assume every convert follows Amani warfare or that a current victim exists.

10.label: Far'atali
10.nativeMeaning: Bloody rites sit close to the boundary of other Loa sects’ heresy; Mueh’zala is the faith’s ominous death patron.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Shrine of the Night’s Friend
scenes.availability: the locality follows Far'atali. A sheltered local shrine or lower temple chamber in a Far’atali settlement. An outer petition step receives visitors. Actual prisoners, a blood rite or a manifestation of Mueh’zala require present circumstances.
scenes.art: Build a squat, ominous death shrine behind angular carved jaws and dark red hanging cloth. A local tablet bears Mueh’zala’s ancient titles, with a heavy blood-offering basin below it and narrow channels cut into the altar’s worn lip. Lidded jars, broad ritual knives and bone charms sit within the keeper’s recess. Shielded lamps make amber pools around the public petition step while the inner idol remains partly lost in shadow. Give this faith a demanding, predatory sacred presence, distinct from Bwonsamdi’s grinning ancestor shrine. The structure can be modest or elaborate in the local culture’s material, with no desert skyline required and no living god or prisoner in the baseline.
contexts: Dark red cloth hangs over a basin grooved for blood offerings. The tablet above names Mueh’zala as God of Death, Father of Sleep, Son of Time and the Night’s Friend. Bone charms cast sharp shadows across covered jars in the keeper’s recess. These observances stand close to what other Loa sects call heresy, and gifts to the death patron are handled beyond the outer petition step. That step gives a visitor space to speak about a vow, an offering or the price demanded, under the unlit stare of the carved idol.
scenes.adaptation: Use local stone or timber and climate-appropriate roofing. Sand, tomb pyramids and Zul’Farrak’s exact cemetery are regional treatments rather than universal necessities.
scenes.purpose: Petitions, dread, bargaining over offerings and friction with rival Loa traditions; the space supplies danger without forcing a sacrifice.
scenes.lore: Native Far’atali description names Mueh’zala and bloody rites. His ancient titles and fearful sacrifice demands appear in Warcraft lore.
scenes.extrapolation: The local tablet is a new inscription of the patron’s titles, not the original Tablet of Theka. The offering chamber and channels are plausible fittings for the mod’s explicit bloody practice.

10.nativeMeaning: A moon-centered Loa tradition whose resemblance to night-elven worship suggests a link between Loa religion and Elunism. Its native faith definition also retains the bloody feast tenet.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Lunar Loa Circle
scenes.availability: the locality follows Rush'atali. An open-sky local shrine courtyard, clearing or roof terrace. Open sky is part of the venue. Day and night lighting follow actual scene time; a reflective basin is ordinary water without automatic moonwell enchantment.
scenes.art: Set crescent-marked shrine posts around a quiet open patch of ground, their beast masks turned upward toward a deliberately clear view of the sky. A shallow offering basin provides a reflective surface at the center, with pale painted moon symbols and small feather bindings along its rim. Covered feast vessels and a cleaned offering blade rest away from the water. Curve broad seats around the basin while leaving its immediate sacred edge clear. Combine the bold carved forms of Loa worship with a restrained silver, indigo and soft violet palette. Use the actual locale’s paving, roofing and plants; a town terrace or desert court can serve the same purpose as a forest clearing. Any light in the basin is reflection from the current sky or nearby lamps.
contexts: Crescent marks run across the shrine posts above a shallow basin. Their beast faces look toward the open sky, linking familiar Loa forms to the moon’s place in Rush’atali worship. Pale symbols follow the basin’s rim, while feather bindings stir over the curved gathering seats. A cleaned offering blade and covered ritual feast bowls stand apart from the water. Offerings can be placed from the clear outer edge. The open center lends itself to shared observance, quiet debate about the moon or an exchange between devotees of related traditions. Water reflects the sky as it presently stands above the court.
scenes.adaptation: Use the host culture’s materials and ordinary local vegetation. Keep the basin shallow and modest; an arid courtyard may hold a tended bowl rather than an abundant spring.
scenes.purpose: Lunar observance, interfaith discussion with Elune devotees, offerings and intimate outdoor conversation.
scenes.lore: The GoA2 description explicitly connects Rushani moon worship with Elunism and Loa religion. No independently corroborated Warcraft institution under this faith name was found. Its native bloody feast tenet distinguishes this from a simple copy of a night-elven devotional court.
scenes.extrapolation: The lunar circle, shrine masks, reflection basin and seats are a modest scene extrapolated directly from the mod’s theology. It is not an established canon Rushani ritual or an automatically magical Elune moonwell. The feast fittings represent that native tenet at rest rather than generating a current rite.

10.label: Hakkari
10.nativeMeaning: The Blood God grants power in exchange for sacrificed souls; other Loa pantheons outlaw his worship.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Altar of the Soulflayer
scenes.availability: the locality follows Hakkari. A Hakkari settlement’s local temple court or guarded inner shrine. County Hakkari faith makes a local altar plausible. Outsiders address the receiving platform; admission behind its rail is controlled. Current sacrifice or summoning requires a separate event.
scenes.art: Make the central idol a vicious winged serpent looming over a broad altar, with a crested head, hooked jaws and sweeping feather-like wings in the unmistakable silhouette of Hakkar. Deep crimson cloth covers the platform’s sides; channels and a collecting basin make its purpose plainly legible. Covered blood vessels, bone ornaments and ceremonial blades occupy a guarded preparation alcove. Warm red lamp light cuts into dark turquoise shadow without requiring glowing spell circles. Place a low receiving platform outside the altar rail, large enough for petitioners and intermediaries. The host culture supplies walls and roof, but the iconography, instruments and division between promised power and its bloody price stay central.
contexts: The winged serpent’s hooked jaws hang over an altar cut with draining channels. Crimson cloth, covered blood vessels and bone-feather ornaments crowd the guarded sacred platform. This is Hakkar’s shrine, where the promise of power is bound to offerings of blood and souls. The receiving floor stops at a rail below the altar; petitions and proposed gifts pass through those who control the inner steps. Lamp smoke gathers under the carved wings, and the preparation alcove keeps its vessels close at hand. The altar itself stands clear for whatever the present gathering brings.
scenes.adaptation: Build the shrine in local materials and scale. Keep the Soulflayer’s winged-serpent motif, blood offering equipment and hierarchical access; no Sunken Temple ruin or Zul’Gurub skyline travels with it.
scenes.purpose: Petitioning for power, negotiating a terrible price, discussing loyalty or defecting; physical danger and doctrine remain visible without scripting victims.
scenes.lore: GoA2 explicitly describes sacrificed souls and the Blood God’s outlawed status elsewhere. Warcraft Hakkari/Atal’ai altars and rituals use blood to feed attempted manifestations.
scenes.extrapolation: The ordinary local guarded altar and reception rail are an authored portable form. It does not reproduce a unique summoning focus, the Egg of Hakkar, a current avatar or a general ban inside its own faithful county.

scenes.label: Shelter of the Protective Coil
scenes.availability: the locality follows Sethrali. A local shrine courtyard or public refuge adjoining an inhabited settlement. Ordinary water and shelter are sufficient. The shrine depicts Sethraliss; her living avatar, original bones, supernatural healing and actual rebirth require current world evidence.
scenes.art: An immense crafted cobra hood shelters the shrine face, with an encircling carved coil forming a protective low boundary around the court. Turquoise inlay, warm gold accents and gently curving paths recall Sethraliss’s original visual language without requiring a monumental sandstone temple. Place clean resting mats, a drinking vessel and a small offering shelf under the shelter, making a visitor’s refuge physically evident. A stylized serpent faces outward as guardian while its coils embrace the gathering space. Use the local culture’s building craft and the current biome around it. The water is ordinary tended water, the hood is made by devotees, and the resting places invite shelter rather than promise a miracle.
contexts: A carved serpent coil encloses the resting court beneath a broad hood. Turquoise marks follow its scales around clean mats and a tended drinking vessel. The shrine honors Sethraliss as a mother and guardian, remembered for the sacrifice through which she protected her people. An offering shelf stands within the coil; the outward-facing serpent watches the public entrance. Travelers can rest beneath the shelter or speak with a keeper beside the water. The enclosing curve makes a small protected space within the surrounding settlement, with the guardian’s image clearly visible from the approach.
scenes.adaptation: Use local stone, wood or metal for the serpent hood. Adapt the shelter to shade, rain or cold; a well-tended urn can replace the basin where water is scarce.
scenes.purpose: Refuge, gratitude, protective obligations, travel assistance and discussion of the Loa’s remembered sacrifice or campaign-appropriate rebirth.
scenes.lore: The mod explicitly describes maternal guardianship and sacrificial protection. Canon sethrak devote temples and prayer to Sethraliss; her original skeleton and avatar are specific sacred presences.
scenes.extrapolation: The modest shelter, drinking vessel and resting court are an extrapolation of protective mother worship, not a documented standardized hospital or magical healing spring.

scenes.label: Hearth of Ariwo’s Covenant
scenes.availability: the locality follows Ariwi. A settlement gathering shelter, caravan stopping yard or modest shared faith house. A stationary local shelter is suitable wherever the county adopts Ariwi. A caravan, vulpera population or living fox deity is not required.
scenes.art: Make a fox-emblem shrine the focal point of a warm, industrious common shelter. Its long ears and curling tail frame a shared hearth rather than a throne. Lidded supply bins, patched blankets, a repair bench and a guest resting place give the faith’s covenant a practical presence; small tokens or offered goods gather on a shrine shelf. Where vulpera culture is present, ingenious salvaged fittings and colorful caravan cloth supply its resourceful original character. Elsewhere keep the local settlement’s normal construction and scale, with the fox emblem marking what has spread. 10.label: Torgi
10.nativeMeaning: A wise and benevolent turtle Loa whose followers travel to hear his stories and preserve or pass them onward.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Story-Keeper’s Shelter
scenes.availability: the locality follows Torgi. A local Torgi shrine, gathering house or shaded settlement court. A local storyteller or visitor can use the space; Torga’s actual presence or a uniquely authenticated scroll is not assumed.
scenes.art: Set a turtle-shell shrine emblem above a broad circle of storytelling seats, with a low open floor where a teller can stand and a flat side surface for maps or keepsakes. Scroll cases, wrapped tablets, ink pots and tracing boards give the stories a durable material life. Use warm amber lamplight, sea-green cloth and generous rounded shapes, evoking the patient richness of tortollan traditions rather than a silent scholar’s library. The shelter can be carved timber, local masonry or canvas in the surrounding culture’s style. Keep its roof dry and its center uncluttered, with broad aisles for traveling packs. Torga is represented by the emblem; the remembered stories carry his presence.
contexts: The turtle-shell emblem hangs above a circle of broad seats. Scroll cases and wrapped tablets fill the dry shelf, with a tracing board laid ready beside maps and keepsakes. Followers honor Torga by carrying stories onward from one listener to another. The central floor gives a tale room to gather an audience; the side table allows a traveler to show the object or route behind it. Warm light catches the worn edges of opened cases. An old account, a disputed memory or news from the road can find attentive space here.
scenes.adaptation: Use local roofing and writing materials. A shell-patterned emblem is crafted; no real giant shell or tortollan body type is required. Scale seats to actual occupants while preserving the broad storyteller circle.
scenes.purpose: Storytelling, intelligence carried by travelers, contested memories, teaching and comparison of records or souvenirs.
scenes.lore: Torga’s wisdom and pilgrimages are native mod theology. Warcraft quest dialogue says pilgrims listen to his stories and pass them to others; tortollans also use and collect scrolls.
scenes.extrapolation: The local shrine-story shelter and its records are portable extrapolations from storytelling and pilgrimage. It is not Torga’s actual shell-side audience site.

scenes.label: Torga’s Pilgrim Rest
scenes.availability: the locality follows Torgi. A settlement-side pilgrim shelter or stopping house on an ordinary road or water landing. Available as a modest local rest venue wherever the county is Torgi and traveling access is plausible. The site need not lie on a route to Torga’s current physical location.
scenes.art: Create a comfortable local pilgrim shelter beneath a turtle-marked lintel, with resting mats set away from the wet or dusty threshold and sturdy shelves protecting traveling packs. A covered water vessel, mended walking staffs and a small route board make the stopping place useful. Place one broad meeting table near the entry for comparing roads, exchanging news and passing on a tale before travelers retire. A few rolled accounts and shell-patterned tokens link hospitality to Torga’s followers without filling every corner with sacred statues. Local carpentry or masonry determines the building; bright travel cloth and warm round-edged furnishings provide its approachable, well-used character.
contexts: The turtle mark above the threshold identifies a stopping place for Torga’s pilgrims. Packs rest on raised shelves, and dry mats lie beyond the drinking vessel. A route board and several rolled accounts occupy the entry table, where travelers can compare a difficult crossing or pass on a story heard elsewhere. Staffs show fresh repairs near the door. The deeper resting corner is screened from arrivals, allowing hosts to receive new callers while earlier guests sleep. Hospitality here keeps the faith’s journeys and its circulating memories moving through the wider world.
scenes.adaptation: Retain the host culture’s normal guesthouse materials and travel methods. Shell-painted canvas or boat fittings are optional; the shared pilgrim welcome and story-exchange objects define the religious venue.
scenes.purpose: Hosting visitors, route choices, travel news, private rest and the practical costs of pilgrimage.
scenes.lore: Native Torgi faith makes pilgrimage a frequent observance. Warcraft depicts tortollan pilgrims journeying to hear and circulate Torga’s stories.
scenes.extrapolation: A local faith-associated stopping house is a modest logistical extrapolation; it does not create a new universally mandated pilgrimage route or a particular age/state of Torga.

10.label: Frghlaith
10.nativeMeaning: An adaptable water pantheon communes with sea powers and takes impressive nearby aquatic creatures as changeable living symbols. Its native definition includes communal identity and bloody feasts.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Shrine of the Changing Waters
scenes.availability: the locality follows Frghlaith. An inhabited shore, riverbank, lake margin or settlement water court. Use an actual local water source or a modest tended basin. Current living sacred creatures are not spawned; their pictured symbol is selected from current local aquatic ecology or follower reports.
scenes.art: A low water-side shrine carries a deliberately replaceable emblem: a swift fish, toothed shark or coiling water beast painted on a removable board or carved plaque. Shell cords and small bone rattles hang above an offering ledge washed by splashes or kept damp beside a basin. Older emblems rest under the shelter, showing that the pantheon changes rather than presenting one eternal fixed image. Covered communal feast vessels wait at one side. Use brilliant shell interiors, iridescent aquatic colors and rough tactile fittings, with a firm visitor shelf at the wet edge. The local culture supplies construction and the actual environment supplies water; the shrine honors encountered creatures without imprisoning or summoning one.
contexts: A fresh aquatic emblem hangs over the wet offering ledge, while older fish and serpent images lie beneath the shelter. Shell cords click above a shallow basin. The shrine’s symbols change with the water creatures that command local notice, so a new visitor’s account of the sea can matter alongside an established offering. Covered communal feast vessels and a cleaned offering knife wait beneath the shrine. The firm outer shelf keeps conversation clear of the slick sacred edge. Water carries small reflections across the current emblem; gifts, observations and disagreements about which creature deserves reverence have a visible place to gather.
scenes.adaptation: Murloc twig-and-mud construction is an optional culture version. Adapt ordinary local building craft and aquatic symbols to the current coast, freshwater environment or inland worship of the sea.
scenes.purpose: Aquatic travel accounts, offerings, shifting religious symbols and disputes over a newly encountered creature’s significance.
scenes.lore: Native Frghlaith explicitly describes communion with water, changeable pantheons and living aquatic symbols. It adopts religious framing found in Warcraft RPG accounts summarized by the wiki. Its native bloody feast tenet supports the ceremonial vessels and idle blade.
scenes.extrapolation: The removable emblem and retired-symbol shelter make that native theology visible as a portable venue. No common fixed god, captive sacred animal or universal ocean temple is asserted.

10.label: Arkkoroc
10.nativeMeaning: A sea demigod who protects followers and tests their faith through violent water and storms; his personal residence remains in Azshara.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Sea-Giant’s Offering Shrine
scenes.availability: the locality follows Arkkoroc. A coastal settlement’s shrine or an inland water court maintained by Arkkoroc’s faithful. Use a sea-facing ledge where present, or a tended basin and sea-giant depiction inland. Storm imagery is symbolic; current weather, Arkkoroc himself and his unique relics are separate facts.
scenes.art: Build a broad, heavy sea-giant image above wave-patterned stone or timber relief. Its powerful shoulders and stern face carry the scale of Arkkoroc’s origin even in a modest shrine. Shell offerings and water vessels occupy a low ledge; dark sea-green cloth and pale sea-foam marks frame a sheltered petition rail. On a coast, orient the opening toward actual surf and weathered rock. Inland, retain a small reflective basin and the same wave relief within the host culture’s ordinary court. Let ropes and stout fittings suggest endurance through water’s violence. This is a local representation of a distant protector, never a duplicated resident giant or transplanted Temple of Arkkoran.
contexts: The sea-giant image stands above carved waves and a ledge of shell offerings. Dark green cloth encloses the petition rail, where a water vessel catches the available light. Arkkoroc is honored as protector and tester, with the violence of tide and tempest given a place in the shrine’s heavy forms. A visitor can bring an account of a dangerous crossing or a promise of thanks to the outer ledge. Stout fittings and worn offering surfaces keep the space practical as well as sacred, while the patron’s distant presence is carried by his crafted image.
scenes.adaptation: Use local construction and keep sea origin legible through carved waves and the patron’s image. Inland versions use a basin; actual salt spray, surf and giant-sized architecture only belong where appropriate.
scenes.purpose: Maritime vows, survival accounts, fear of storms and petitions to a distant patron; dry inland worship remains physically plausible.
scenes.lore: GoA2 explicitly establishes protection and tempest tests. The canonical sea giant resides at the Temple of Arkkoran; the surrounding religion’s fuller framing is RPG-derived and adopted by the mod.
scenes.extrapolation: The local sea-giant offering shrine and basin are faithful portable extrapolations. The patron, his sons, original temple and Heart of Arkkoroc are not replicated.

10.label: Oraclism
10.nativeMeaning: Guardians honor and tend Titan technology without properly understanding it; their religious relationship includes gathering shiny offerings.
10.sourceDecision: The native faith has a distinctive observance or social practice that supports the attached modest local venue.

scenes.label: Shiny Offering Shelter
scenes.availability: the locality follows Oraclism. A local Oraclism settlement shrine or community shelter. A simple symbolic shrine is portable. An authentic Titan fragment, functioning Great Stone or machine appears only where already evidenced; this base has none.
scenes.art: Make a small, exuberant offering shelter filled with treasures whose appeal is their shine: polished pebbles, bright shell, odd metal buttons, beads and bits of colored glass. A handmade shrine marker copies angular patterns remembered from the Great Stones, visibly painted or carved by local hands. Keep offered treasures on a protected shelf and incoming finds on a sorting mat, with a clear guest spot beside them. Humble fittings contrast with the solemn importance assigned to this jumble. Gorloc versions use rounded little shelters and leafy shade; other converts keep their own architecture. No object is a glowing power source or authentic Titan machine merely because the faithful cherish it.
contexts: Bright pebbles, metal trinkets and colored glass crowd the offering shelf around a handmade geometric shrine marker. A sorting mat holds newly gathered finds, each cleaned enough to catch the light. The Oracles’ reverence for the Great Stones lives here in gifts and copied marks, even when the mechanisms behind those sacred forms remain mysterious. A guest can show a discovery beside the mat or question why one shiny piece deserves pride of place. The protected shelf distinguishes offerings from ordinary possessions without revealing any hidden machine or divine response.
scenes.adaptation: Use the current culture’s building scale and materials. Low gorloc shelters and broad jungle leaves are optional original-culture art. The copied geometric marker is explicitly handmade, and the offerings are ordinary local finds.
scenes.purpose: Sharing discoveries, friendly requests for offerings, misunderstood ancient symbols and discussion of guardianship; genuine relic investigation can use an independently evidenced location variant.
scenes.lore: Native Oraclism describes misunderstood Titan guardianship. Gods like Shiny Things and Appeasing the Great Rain Stone explicitly involve gathered shiny shrine offerings.
scenes.extrapolation: A handmade symbolic shrine beyond Sholazar is an extrapolation for a faith that has spread. No Great Rain Stone, Titan relic, jungle habitat or working technology is assumed to exist in every converted county.

10.label: Velenism
10.nativeMeaning: Velen carries K'ure's naaru teachings through the draenei exile: Faith, Courage and Heart, virtuous conduct, and protection of the dead from demons and the Void.
10.sourceDecision: Light teaching, hospitality and guarded funerary space directly serve this faith's native concerns; scale them to a local community rather than reproducing the Exodar or Auchindoun.

scenes.label: The Chapel of Faith, Courage and Heart
scenes.availability: the locality follows Velenism. A suitable inhabited holding, village, travel settlement or local temple precinct with room for a small teaching chapel. Use the current county population faith. A plain adapted room or shaded shrine suffices; no resident naaru, draenei population, spacecraft or magical crystal machinery is required.
scenes.art: Build a welcoming local Light chapel around a faceted radiant emblem and three small panels for Faith, Courage and Heart. Violet-gold lamplight picks out the teaching stand, folded travel blankets, a water vessel and broad guest seating. In a draenei setting, use graceful bronze curves and rose-violet crystal ornament; elsewhere fit the same devotional core into local construction. Leave an open floor for instruction, an accessible receiving table and a screened resting nook. The space should carry the dignity of a people who preserve hope through exile, with their teaching and practical care visibly joined. The emblem represents the naaru; it is a crafted object, with ordinary lamps providing the default light.
contexts: A faceted Light emblem hangs above the teaching stand, catching the chapel's violet and gold lamps. Three small panels name Faith, Courage and Heart. Water cups wait on the receiving table beside folded blankets, while a broad bench gives travelers somewhere to sit with their baggage. A patterned screen shelters a resting nook beyond the open teaching floor. The doorway lets the surrounding settlement remain visible. Lessons, requests for shelter and conversations over a cup can share this room beneath the same radiant emblem.
scenes.adaptation: Keep local walls and furnishings. Draenei communities favor curved bronze and violet facets; human, dwarf or other converts reproduce the emblem and teaching arrangement in their own stone, timber, cloth and scale.
scenes.purpose: Instruction, welcome, charitable support and discussion of difficult choices; visitors may use the public receiving side and seek access to the resting nook.
scenes.lore: Native description names the three values and the history of exile; draenei Light custodians safeguard altars and teach the naaru's path.
scenes.extrapolation: A small teaching/refuge chapel, three panels and its guest fittings are practical local extrapolations. Lamp colors and ornament are visual translations, not a miraculous property.

scenes.label: The Guarded Court of the Honored Dead
scenes.availability: the locality follows Velenism. A settlement burial ground, temple memorial court or modest local crypt accessible to visitors. Ordinary grave protection and remembrance follow current local faith. Visible spirits, soul-binding crystals, awakened vigilants or a functioning magical ward require separate current facts.
scenes.art: Create a small sacred burial court whose central visual promise is guardianship of the dead. Pale radiant marks repeat on closed grave covers and a sheltered memorial wall; warm lanterns burn between names, simple flower vessels and neatly maintained stone. Curved bronze or locally worked metal frames the entry. Give the inner graves dignity and enclosure, with a remembrance ledge and room for visitors to leave a token outside the sealed doors. Draenei versions can carry luminous-looking facets and alien curves; other cultures keep their own tomb construction. The court is a local expression of soul protection, not a miniature city of the dead. Its default illumination comes from lamps, and all burials remain closed.
contexts: Radiant marks repeat above the closed graves and along the memorial wall. Warm lanterns reveal names, flower vessels and small remembrance tokens beneath the sheltering roof. A broad ledge leaves room to set down an offering or unfold a family record. Beyond it, the burial doors remain shut, with the maintained path keeping visitors clear of their hinges. The enclosure quiets the nearby settlement. Custodians can receive requests at the entry while families speak beside the memorials, in a place arranged to keep the honored dead under faithful protection.
scenes.adaptation: Use local burial forms and climate-appropriate enclosure. Draenei motifs may include curved arches and faceted ornament; adopters preserve the protective Light motif without creating a new Auchindoun.
scenes.purpose: Memorial visits, family records, funerary arrangements and petitions to custodians; access to sealed burials is controlled.
scenes.lore: Native Velenism explicitly guards deceased souls. Auchenai duties at Auchindoun include communing with the dead and protecting their souls from harm.

Image direction: Create a small sacred burial court whose central visual promise is guardianship of the dead. Pale radiant marks repeat on closed grave covers and a sheltered memorial wall; warm lanterns burn between names, simple flower vessels and neatly maintained stone. Curved bronze or locally worked metal frames the entry. Give the inner graves dignity and enclosure, with a remembrance ledge and room for visitors to leave a token outside the sealed doors. 10.label: Lightbound
10.nativeMeaning: A zealous naaru-derived doctrine treats universal conversion as the path to unity, peace and justice, accepting coercion to overcome resistance.
10.sourceDecision: A public mission hall expresses the faith's organizing purpose wherever it spreads; no forced-conversion event or visiting army is implied by the setting.

scenes.label: The Hall of the One Radiance
scenes.availability: the locality follows Lightbound. An inhabited holding or settlement able to support a small mission hall, temple room or roofed assembly court. Current local county faith selects the scene. Scale its mission administration to the locality; prisoners, conversions under force, Lightforging and military deployments are separate events.
scenes.art: Create a forceful Lightbound mission hall with a single faceted radiant emblem dominating the teaching platform. White and gold banners repeat it down an unusually ordered approach. An oath desk, copies of teachings and a map marked with the mission's destinations make the room both devotional and administrative. Put public benches near the entry and a narrower side office for petitions or recruitment records. Draenei versions use burnished geometric metal and severe crystalline ornament; converts use local architecture beneath the same emphatic motif. Bright lamps and controlled sightlines present unity as something carefully assembled and extended outward. The image contains the instruments of conversion, without depicting a captive, named exarch, summoned naaru or compulsory ceremony.
contexts: The same radiant emblem repeats along the hall's pale banners, drawing the eye toward the teaching platform. Benches face it in straight rows. An oath desk holds open copies of the doctrine and a stack of blank records; beside it, a mission map marks destinations beyond the settlement. The entry keeps arriving visitors visible to the platform, while a side office allows a closer conversation. Here the faith is taught as a single answer meant to reach the wider world. Questions, petitions and terms of service can be heard before the assembled symbols of that purpose.
scenes.adaptation: Local culture supplies the hall and furniture; the repeated single emblem, orderly approach and mission records carry Lightbound identity. Use a few benches in a village and a larger assembly floor in a city.
scenes.purpose: Teaching, conversion inquiries, mission negotiations and recruitment; public entry does not require a visitor to agree or convert.
scenes.lore: Native doctrine and the alternate-Draenor Lightbound both emphasize universal conversion and unity, including force.
scenes.extrapolation: The specific hall, mission map and oath desk are portable institutional extrapolation; the static room never performs conversion or establishes a particular historical army.

10.label: Maldraxxi
10.nativeMeaning: A death cult draws power from Maldraxxus and is distinguished by necromancers assembling abominations from many corpses' limbs and parts. Human sacrifice and warmongering are declared native tenets, so the workshop should retain ominous bodily-extraction affordances as well as stitching.
10.sourceDecision: Fleshcraft preparation is explicitly native practice and merits a characteristic workshop wherever the cult is established, using mortal-world scale and materials.

scenes.label: The Flesh-Stitching House
scenes.availability: the locality follows Maldraxxi. A settled holding with a sheltered workroom, crypt workshop or outbuilding suited to necromantic craft and controlled visitor access. Local faith can supply the ordinary preparation venue. A visibly animated abomination, captive, fresh killing or soul transfer requires a current scene/event fact.
scenes.art: Give the Maldraxxi cult a grotesquely practical fleshcraft workshop: broad slabs with binding rings, black iron hooks, thick stitching needles, tendon-colored cords and shelves of sorted bone. Covered bundles and a partially assembled inert patchwork form show exactly what this craft handles. Riblike braces and green glass lamps echo Maldraxxus without transforming the surrounding land into the Shadowlands. A receiving bench stands beside a work slate recording sizes and parts beside an empty extraction slab; it gives admitted visitors a view of the craft beyond a low partition. Use heavy, stained surfaces and severe functional light rather than a theatrical sacrificial altar. The horror comes from bodies treated as material and workmanship; nothing in the default image is moving or receiving a new soul.
contexts: Thick needles and coils of cord lie beside the oversized slab. Binding rings and extraction tools occupy an empty side slab; bone pieces fill trays beneath hanging hooks, and covered bundles fill the shelves beyond them. An unfinished patchwork form rests motionless under a coarse cloth, its mismatched outline visible at the edge. Green glass lamps catch the iron braces and old stains in the work surface. A receiving bench and a slate of measurements occupy the near side of the partition. Visitors can discuss a commission, inspect the workmanship or question the custodian without stepping between the slabs.
scenes.adaptation: Use local walls, weatherproofing and furniture, with the same unmistakable patchwork craft at the core. Rural versions use one slab and a few shelves; urban versions can have several stations.
scenes.purpose: Necromantic commissions, work inspection, provision disputes or philosophical confrontation; admission ends at the receiving partition unless custodians permit more.
scenes.lore: Native description identifies assembled abominations. Blizzard describes Maldraxxus bodies constructed from selected flesh and bone and an Abomination Factory. Native tenets explicitly permit human sacrifice and warmongering; dormant extraction fittings preserve that darker practice.
scenes.extrapolation: A local mortal cult stitch-house and its receiving arrangements are extrapolated from that explicit craft. Shadowlands houses, anima supplies and living necrotic geography are not assumed.

10.label: Throsi
10.nativeMeaning: Throsi bind dead souls into durable constructs using death magic mixed with corrupted druidic elements; witch covens extend the practice among living communities.
10.sourceDecision: Effigies, wicker/wood construct frames and knot charms are an exceptionally strong portable motif. Keep the standard venue a preparation space rather than declaring every settlement possessed.

scenes.label: The Coven's Bone-and-Willow Yard
scenes.availability: the locality follows Throsi. A sheltered courtyard, shed, cave entrance or enclosed garden within a suitable inhabited locality. Current local faith can support a coven preparation venue. Constructs remain inert; curses, trapped spirits, an active coven ritual, a Matron or an entrance to Thros require current evidence.
scenes.art: Create an intimate Throsic craft yard where tall willow-and-root bodies lean under shelter, their angular shoulders tied with bone and coarse dark cord. Animal skull charms, antler forks and carved wooden faces hang above a worktable of knot bindings. A blackened stone recess holds the empty heart sockets for the larger frames, unmistakably suggesting where death magic would anchor them. Place a low receiving stool beside the approach and leave a distinct path through the yard. Its local walls and vegetation remain visible around this invasive woodland craft. Materials should feel rough, damp or weathered according to the region; the effigy silhouette supplies the faith's horror. All frames and charms remain ordinary still objects in the base scene.
contexts: Willow-and-root frames lean beneath the shelter, their long shoulders bound with pale bone and dark cord. Carved faces wait on the worktable beside antler forks and coils of binding material. Skull charms hang above an inner recess where empty heart sockets have been laid out for fitting. The receiving stool stands beside a clear path through the yard. Wind stirs the loose cords while the larger bodies remain still. A visitor can bring a request to the table, examine a charm or speak with the custodian under the patient shapes of unfinished constructs.
scenes.adaptation: Harvest locally suitable wood or traded wicker; deserts can use thornwood and cord, snowlands dense timber under a roof, and cities an enclosed craft court. Preserve the local building around the cult fittings.
scenes.purpose: Covens' consultations, craft requests, scrutiny of charms and contested local practices; the binding recess is an inner preparation area.
scenes.lore: Native description specifies soul-bound durable constructs and witch covens. Warcraft wicker constructs combine wood, bones and other dead material; heart charms anchor their spirits.
scenes.extrapolation: A recurring local preparation yard, receiving stool and material storage are authored. Its still craft apparatus does not establish possession or an active curse.

10.label: Helism
10.nativeMeaning: Helya rules Helheim and gathers souls through the Kvaldir and Helarjar, her deathly counterparts to Odyn's warriors; her cult joins death, servitude and the sea. Its coded gruesome-festival tenet also warrants a grim communal feast setting, distinct from mortuary remembrance.
10.sourceDecision: A local keel shrine or boat-shaped mortuary is a defensible portable expression of Helya's maritime death cult. It neither opens Helheim nor produces supernatural mist.

scenes.label: The Black-Keel Shrine
scenes.availability: the locality follows Helism. A village, inhabited holding or temple precinct with a modest mortuary/shrine area; use a landing or shore-side building when water is locally available. Inland settlements use a crafted keel marker and vessel-shaped shrine on dry ground. A real cursed fleet, Kvaldir, soul-capturing lantern or supernatural sea fog is a separate current state.
scenes.art: Shape a Helist mortuary shrine around an upright black keel and a low boat-form bier beneath a relief of the sea-witch. Heavy chains, hooked iron, shell lamps and plaques for the lost give it an unmistakably maritime death cult identity. Weathered wood, dark blue-green cloth and severe stone make the atmosphere cold without adding magical fog. A sheltered outer bench faces the shrine while keeping the closed bier and deeper memorial chamber distinct. At a coast, frame the arrangement with an ordinary landing and actual water; inland, the same keel is a crafted symbol housed in local architecture. The sea-witch is depicted in an image, and the shrine holds neither her Soulcage nor a doorway to Helheim.
contexts: An upright black keel rises above the closed boat-shaped bier. Hooked chain hangs beside a relief of the sea-witch, its links catching the shell lamps' low light. Names of the lost fill plaques along the inner wall. Dark cloth covers the bier, with a bowl for memorial tokens set on the outer ledge. The sheltered bench faces the shrine without entering the deeper chamber. Here visitors can arrange remembrance, ask about the fate of the dead or speak over a pledge beneath a faith whose sea gathers souls as well as ships.
scenes.adaptation: Retain local stone and building silhouettes. Coastal communities use real worn timbers and mooring hardware; inland converts carry the keel/chain iconography into a dry enclosed shrine rather than gaining a sea.
scenes.purpose: Mortuary requests, memorials, pledges and discussion of the cult's claims; visitors remain in the public outer shrine unless admitted inward.
scenes.lore: Native Helya lore and Kvaldir descriptions join her authority, maritime raiding and the gathering of souls for Helheim.
scenes.extrapolation: Ubiquitous local keel shrine, boat-form bier and memorial fittings are authored iconographic extrapolations; neither an established canonical rite nor actual soul capture is asserted.

scenes.label: The Sea-Witch's Death-Feast Hall
scenes.availability: the locality follows Helism. A settled holding, local temple precinct or substantial village with a roofed feast room. Use current local faith and the current gruesome-festival practice. Static feast fittings require no festival date. Actual victims, fresh trophies, Kvaldir guests or a summoned soul require current event support.
scenes.art: Make a Helist feast hall where a long keel-shaped table runs below chain-hung lamps and death-mask standards. Skull-carved cups, heavy serving boards and empty trophy hooks turn communal celebration toward grim triumph and the sea-witch's claim over death. A relief of Helya occupies the raised seat's back, with dark blue-green cloth behind it. A vrykul version can be enormous, built of ship timber and weathered iron; other cultures use their own hall and proportions. Keep an outer visitor bench and a clear passage beside the table. The festive apparatus should feel threatening and theatrical without supplying fresh corpses or a compulsory gruesome event. The place can host ordinary audience and anticipation between festivals.
contexts: The long table narrows into a keel-shaped end beneath chain-hung lamps. Skull-carved cups and heavy serving boards lie below death-mask standards, with empty trophy hooks along the wall. A relief of the sea-witch marks the raised seat's back. The outer bench leaves visitors apart from the table's place of honor, while a clear passage follows its length. Talk can carry across the whole hall or gather beneath one lamp. The feast fittings give victory and death a communal stage, waiting for whatever gathering the current hosts choose to hold.
scenes.adaptation: Preserve local architecture and normal head/body scale. Vrykul versions use heavy ship timber and huge benches; inland or smaller converts keep the keel, chains and death-mask motifs in their own hall.

10.label: Ebon Blade
10.nativeMeaning: Freed death knights develop a worldview suited to undeath, organize around the Ebon Blade and defend their world after escape from the Lich King's control.
10.sourceDecision: An austere local muster armoury makes their practical identity visible without turning every converted village into Acherus or assuming that all residents are death knights.

scenes.label: The Armoury of the Free Blade
scenes.availability: the locality follows Ebon Blade. A settled holding or temple/civic precinct with a small hall or covered muster room. Use current local county faith. This is a local adherent institution, not an automatic official chapter, Acherus, Death Gate, working runeforge or raised army; exceptional magical apparatus needs current support.
scenes.art: Design a local Ebon adherent armoury around a dark blade emblem, heavy weapon racks and a rune-etched maintenance bench. Cold blue lamps pick out black steel, repaired straps and records of watches and service. The room is martial and severe, with space for a small muster and a separate visitor strip beside the bench. In a death-knight settlement, their distinctive runeblades and massive plate can furnish the racks; other adherents keep equipment appropriate to current occupants while preserving the same emblem and practical arrangements. Use the local hall's walls rather than manufacturing a flying necropolis. Rune marks are visible craftsmanship; the default bench is not an operating soul forge, and the open doorway offers an ordinary route outside.
contexts: A dark blade emblem hangs above the weapon racks. Cold blue lamps reveal repaired straps, rune-cut metal and a broad maintenance bench with space for a sheathed sword. Muster records occupy a separate desk beside the cleared visitor strip. The hall's center is left open for instruction or a small assembly. Metal sounds carry from the working side, while the entry remains visible from the desk. Admitted visitors can bring a request, examine equipment or discuss service in a room arranged around the work of defenders who claim their own will.
scenes.adaptation: Keep local construction and practical scale. The emblem and rune-marked martial tools carry the faith; human or dwarf converts need no Scourge necropolis architecture.
scenes.purpose: Service petitions, defence discussions, martial instruction and equipment inspection; visitors use the reception strip and do not gain weapon or forge access automatically.
scenes.lore: Native faith centers freed death knights and defence. Runeblades and runeforging are distinctive Ebon/death-knight craft, but functioning runeforges have specific game locations.
scenes.extrapolation: A local armoury and maintenance bench are extrapolated. This purposefully scales down the motif rather than distributing canonical runeforge infrastructure to every faith locality.

10.label: Nazen
10.nativeMeaning: Nazen teaches renunciation of emotion, placing society above the individual and accepting self-sacrifice for the common good. Its native tenets combine communal identity, literalism and human sacrifice; the sacrificial practice is part of the mod faith even though the description emphasizes renunciation and common duty.
10.sourceDecision: A common-service teaching hall expresses the native philosophy, while a separate sacrificial precinct preserves its coded darker practice without making a death occur on entry.

scenes.label: The Hall of Common Service
scenes.availability: the locality follows Nazen. An inhabited holding or village with a shared room, roofed work shelter or civic assembly court. Select by current local county faith; occupants follow current culture and character state. No automatic sacrifice, caste conversion or removal of individual emotion is performed.
scenes.art: Create an austerely arranged community hall with a broad shared work surface, tablets of duties, plain resource compartments and an instruction stand. The room's strongest visual choice is what receives prominence: communal work and provision rather than personal trophies or devotional idols. Furniture repeats in practical, uniform forms with clear routes between tools, records and teaching space. In a nerubian locality, use polished angular stone, silk supports and wall-mounted fittings; elsewhere express the same common-service arrangement through local carpentry or masonry. Preserve useful visitor seating beside the records. Spare lamps reveal material workmanship without luxurious display. This is an extrapolated gathering place for a native social philosophy, not an established Warcraft temple design or an compulsory scene of self-sacrifice.
contexts: Duty tablets face the shared work surface. Spare tools and provision compartments line the wall, each within reach of the clear central floor. Plain seats turn toward an instruction stand without a throne, idol or display of personal trophies. A smaller table beside the records gives visitors somewhere to present a request. 10.label: Moonweaver
10.nativeMeaning: Moonweavers worship Arachelune, an Elune offshoot depicted as a spider goddess who demands absolute obedience and fealty. Native tenets also prescribe moon worship, human sacrifice and ritual cannibalism, making her worship darker than a simple spider-themed Elunic shrine.
10.sourceDecision: A moon-and-web fealty shrine follows the mod's direct imagery; an Elunic moonwell's magical function is not transferred merely because the faith is an offshoot.

scenes.label: The Moonweaver's Web of Fealty
scenes.availability: the locality follows Moonweaver. A settlement shrine, local temple room, sheltered courtyard or cave-edge chapel. Current local county faith selects the scene. Arachelune appears only as a crafted depiction; living spiders, magical webs, divine presence and a functioning Elunic moonwell require separate justification.
scenes.art: Make a striking Moonweaver shrine around a spider goddess image backed by a silver crescent. Eight canopy points carry taut radial threads above the central fealty ledge, framing the goddess as the center of an ordered web. Pale lamps catch fine silk or cord and deep blue-violet cloth; the outer visitor seats sit lower and farther from the focal image. Nerubian settings can integrate the web into walls and overhead approaches; other converts place the same radial motif within their own chapel or courtyard. Keep an accessible outer lane for petitions and observation. This is confident extrapolation from GoA2's Arachelune theology, not borrowed Lolth lore. The threads, canopy and image are material religious fittings.
contexts: A spider goddess image stands before a silver crescent. Taut threads radiate above the central ledge, their eight canopy points catching the pale lamps. Low seats occupy the outer ring, with a clear lane between them and the inward approach. Fine cord and dark cloth make even the smallest movement visible against the shrine's still geometry. A visitor can wait among the outer seats, bring a petition forward or speak beside the fealty ledge. Every strand leads toward the same depicted authority, leaving the meaning of obedience plainly present in the room.
scenes.adaptation: Use silk where available or fine cord as the web motif. Local culture retains its arches, furnishings and body scale; the goddess's spider/moon imagery and inwardly focused hierarchy remain.
scenes.purpose: Petitions, pledges, instruction and encounters with a hierarchical local religious institution; attendance never automatically creates a vow.
scenes.lore: GoA2 description specifically supplies spider-form Arachelune and absolute fealty. Targeted searches located no direct Warcraft canonical Arachelune worship tradition.
scenes.extrapolation: Crescent, radial canopy and fealty ledge are authored readings of the native image and doctrine. No canonical ceremony, moonwell property or imported non-Warcraft spider goddess is asserted.

scenes.art: Create a Moonweaver inner chamber with a crescent-backed spider image above a sacrificial altar, its binding points clearly visible beneath a taut web-pattern canopy. A covered knife rests on a side stand; empty ritual platters and vessels occupy a separate feast ledge. Pale moon-colored lamps and deep blue-violet cloth draw the witness seats into a radial arrangement around these two uses of the room. Keep local architectural forms visible around the cult fittings. contexts: The spider image rises above the altar's binding points, backed by a pale crescent. A covered knife rests on its own stand. Empty platters and vessels line the feast ledge beneath a canopy of taut radial cord. Witness seats face the altar and the ledge together, while the outer screen marks where admitted visitors may stop. Pale lamps reveal both preparations in the quiet chamber. scenes.adaptation: Use local building materials with the same moon/web imagery. Nerubian web-supported seating is cultural; other converts can use stone, timber and fine cord without acquiring arachnid bodies or subterranean cities.
